Report comes from Washington that
the United States Maritime Commission
has approved the application of the
Baltimore Mail Steamship Co. to trans
Ter its five combination passenger and
cargo vessels to the intercoastal serv-
ice. That means a limping revival of
the almost abandoned marine passenger
service between the Atlantic and Pacific
Coasts


Only a year ago this shipping route
through the Panama Canal was highly
popular with coast-to-coast travellers.
There were three lines affording almost
continuous communication and they
were all literally patronized, but now
there remain only the West-bound trips
OF the Dollar Line ships, not more than
fortnightly at best, in connection with
the company's ound-the-world service
The New York-San Francisco schedule
of the Grace Line has been completely
abandoned, and so has the service main
tanned by the Panama-Pacific Line with
Its three luxury ships. California, Penn
sylvania and Virginia.


All that has remained has been the
west bound service of the Dollar Line
and the extremely limited passenger ac-
commodations available on occasional
cargo vessels. The sudden deprivation
has been severely felt by travellers be-
tween the Atlantic Coast and California
who preferred the ease and luxury of
the water route.


The loss will now be partially repaired
by the transfer of the five ships of the
Baltimore line to the intercoastal serv-.
Ice. These vessels have hitherto been
operating between Baltimore and Nor
folk and continental European ports.

WITH SPANISH INSURGENTS
ON THE SARRION FRONT, July l6
P).-Advancing insurgents and gov
ernment defenders were engaged in
a terrific battle in the mountains of
Lower Aragon today.


Through the scrub pine growth of
the rugged mountains of Eastern
Spain the insurgents advanced against
government forces striving desperately
to block Gen. Francisco Frances
drive on Valencia.


Crushed in sanguinary fighting in
the mountains flanking the Teruel-
Sagunto highway about the strategic
villages of Sarrion and Albentosa. the
defenders fell back into the Sierra
ell Toro.


Under constant insurgent artillery
and aerial punishment, the govern
ment fighters apparently were en-
deavoring to establish new defenses
at BARRACKS, on the highway 8 miles
southeast of Albentosa.


The insurgents hammered then way
to the outskirts of Albentos.. which,
with Sarrion, are key points control
ling roads extending northward to q
pocket where large government force
faced threatened encirclemeat.


Since occupation of Manzanera gave
the insurgents possession of the main
Teruel-Sagunto highway south from
Sarrion and Albentosa. the government
force apparently relied on hastily
built mountain trails to effect an
escape


Insurgent airplanes dominated the
air with scores of bombers and lighter
fighting ships maneuvering all day
over government lines, bombing and
machine cunning their entrench-
ments.

SHANGHAI, Dec. 81 (P.-The Jap
anese were reported by foreign
sources today to have rushed troops
into Manchukuo to put down dis
turbances caused by units of China s
9th Route Army which had crossed
into the Japanese-dominated state.


Reports from Peiping said from
IS to 20 train loads of Japanese had
been crossing the border daily at
Shanhaikuan for several days. A
Japanese army spokesman, however
denied that any troops were being
sent into Manchukuo and said no
trouble had been reported anywhere
along the border.


Trouble in F0rmosa.


The Chinese press reported trouble
also was brewing in Formosa where
Formosans and Chinese residents
were opposing Japan's strict war
measures.


Meanwhile, Chinese reported new
victories on the central front and
in North China where the japanese
were sending troop reinforcements
to stamp out guerrilla activities.


Breaking the long deadlock on the
Canton -Hankow Railway, the Chi
nese said they had recaptured Ma
tang Station, miles south of Yo-
chow, gateway to Human Province
inflicting 300 casualties.


They also asserted Chinese guer-
rillas in Shantung Province. North
China, had recaptured Changkiu. 80
miles north of Tsinan, destroying
two railway stations.


5000 Fresh Japanese Arrive.


Three thousand fresh Japanese
troops were said to have arrived at
Linfen, Shansi Province, to reinforce
units now attempting to pacify
Southwestern Shansi.


Reports from Chungking, China S
provisional capital said the Chinese
expected the japanese soon to
launch their projected offensive
across the frozen Yellow River into
Shensi and Ninghsia Provinces In
Northwest China.


Japanese units in ShanSi and Sui
yuan were reported moving into
positions from which they could ad-
vance when the river was sufficient
ly frozen to carry tanks and heavy
artillery.

NEW YORK, May 28.-May
threatens to go down in local history
as the month in which the most extra
special. four-star sports events did not
take place.


First the heralded hoss race between
War Admiral and Seabiscuit came
down with the spavins and now those
two orphans of the storm. Barney Ross
and Henry Armstrong, have been put
off until next Tuesday night. The
weather being what it is, there's no
guarantee they'll fight even then.


The whole thing is about to spoil
Mike Jacobs sunny disposition. Even
if Barney and Henry DO contrive to
sneak in their scheduled IS rounds
Tuesday, there still will remain only
three weeks in which Mike can steam
up the Schmeling-Louis champion
ship on June %.


Bout Forced on Jacobs.


Schmeling and Louis already have
established their training camps and
Schmeling has been boxing for several
days. Louis has taken over Arm
strong's quarters at Pompton Lakes,
leaving his smaller and even darker
Negro friend no place to train except
at Stillman's stuffy gymnasium here,
which belonged to Ross by right Of
prior discovery.


What makes matters worse is that
the Jacobs Office is being swamped
with applications for Schmeling- Louis
tickets, and Mike will have none to sell
until Ross and Armstrong are out Of
the way.


Mike now admits he was forced into
staging the ss-Armstrong this month
against his better judgment. He fig
ured it would draw close to $500, 900
in July.


But Lou Ambers, the lightweight
ruler, beefed to the Boxing Commission
that such an arrangement might de-
prive him of a big outdoor shot against
the winner, and the commission agreed
with him. Now prevailing guess is
that Armstrong and Ross will be lucky
to draw over $l25,00O.


Ross Remains Favorite.


While Barney and Henry swore
mildly and resumed their interrupted
training, Ross still was a sound 80
favorite. Apparently nobody had fig
ured out precisely how the postpone
ment would affect one fighter more
than the other.


Ross seemed pretty vicious and
nearly knocked out a little Negro
named Herbert Solomon, who looked
something like Armstrong, but whose
resemblance ended there. Anyway.
Barney demonstrated that his right
still is damaging punch.

game, but both were due to give their
sparring partners a going over today

There is a new government here

France and Great Britain have

Denied the possibility of continuing
mer former policy, Czechoslovakia
must play the role of Balkan states,
search for Emergencies among her

for any and every advantage.


Must Exploit Her Foes.


Thus, while she faces the threat that
Poland and Hungary may despoil her
utterly of the eastern stretches Of her
country, which reach from Bratislava
through the Carpathians to the juno
ton of Poland and Rumania, Czecho-

Italy would, like to have all this

Germany opposes this, however, it

Consequently, the Czechs are hope

herself will save the Czechs the loss Of
the eastern third of their country.
loss which seems the more important

Indeed, it is the failure of the Slovaks
to rally entirely to Prague in this hour
of peril which makes the new govern
ment, announced today. less national
than it must become, 1t is hoped, after
the meeting tomorrow of the Slovak
Peoples party of the late Father
Andreas Hlinka.


While the Czechs and Slovaks are
of the same race, they have utterly
different cultures, with the formers
bustling bourgeois ways not under
standable to the music-loying Slovaks,
who are still oriental, and it is only
natural that the Slovaks should eX-

Except for this problem and the

new government is really government

ems Gen. Syrovy's hand as he at

its rapacious neighbors and even
tually to ease the modified nation
back into peace-time occupations.


Dr.. Kamil Krofta, Benes' friend.
yields the foreign office after three
years to DR.. Francis Chvalkovsky,
Czech Minister to Rome. A member
of the Agrarian party who had always
pleaded for better relations with Ger
many, DR.. Chvalkovsky has been Min
lister both to Washington and Berlin.


AS the new government thus starts
with a foreign minister who can treat
with the Germans and Italians, Propa-
ganda Minister Hugo Vavrecka has
been sent to Berlin to improve rela-

been blaring out against Prague and
raising the specter of further Ger

selves from the rule of the Jews"

These signs are the more hopeful

These reports are absurd in country
which is bourgeois to the core and
where, as these correspondents of the
Chicago Daily News have discovered,
all the gendarmes have been brought
in from the provinces to make doubly
sure that Prague is secure against any
such efforts.


Those signs are doubly hopeful,
moreover. since the CZechs were con-
fronted Tuesday night with Hun
garlan ultimatu.n which, for all its
effort at friendly language, remains
peremptory. The Hungarians give the
CZechs until clock this afternoon
to hand over Komarom and another
frontier town as token cessions look

"conquests."


The Czechs, consequently, can only
hope that the Germans and British
will demand from the Hungarians
more restraint than the Germans
themselves were willing to show. This
is a strange hope, but recent weeks

diplomacy since the partition of
Poland.

HENDAYE, France. April 2s-An
engagement between the fleets of the
insurgents and the Spanish govern
ment was narrowly avoided, it was
learned today. when insurgent wal
vessels bonabarded government land
forces yesterday.


Dispatches from both sides said the
insurgent war feet, including the
cruisers Canarias and Almirante Ger
vera, together with smaller vessels
rained shells on government lines
along the Mediterranean Wednesday
especially Alcala de Chivert, north of
Castellon.


Loyalist Ships Sent.


Barcelona radio orders sent the
government ships steaming at forced
draft to the area, but their COM
manders declared they arrived too late
to engage the insurgents.


The government feet has been
based at Cartagena. A sea battle off
Cartagena occurred between the two
fleets March 6. The insurgent cruiser
Beleares was torpedoed and sunk with
an estimated loss of 900 lives.


Heavy bombardment OF government
positions at Albocacer, on the coastal
front north of Castellon, was reported
by the insurgent command at Irun
today to have destroyed two trains
OF government reinforcements arriv-
ing from Castellon.


Dispatches from the government
front at Albocacer said the resistance
was growing stronger every hour, and
that the insurgent offensive along the
Aloocacer-Alcala de Chivert line def
nitely was stopped


Threat to Loyalist Rear.


Insurgents said rain drenching all
Eastern Spain prevented their often
sive from developing normally. !"
From the east, however, a new threat
developed toward the government's S
rear.


Gen. Jose Varela's veteran Casti-
lians drove down the highway from
Teruel toward Valencia, aiming at the
coast at Sagunto.


A successful drive would trap the
government troops north of Castellon
in another coastal pocket, such as
that about Barcelona where govern
ment defenders have been cut of
from the rest of Spain


Gen. Varela opened his drive down
the 60-mile highway to Sagunto and
the coast when his troops stormed
government flanking positions in the
Pobo Mountains northeast of Teruel
yesterday.


Fifteen miles down the coast from
Sagunto is Valencia, main supply base
for Central Spain.


The Insurgents difficult task was to
break through the strong system of
government trenches which crisscross
the highway. and then to drive be-
hind the governments front line in
Southern Teruel and Central Castel-
lon.


Varela's success would mean virtual
collapse Of government resistance in
East Central Spain. as the govern
ments entire right wing would be
hemmed in with the Mediterranean at
its rear.

quarter. Deliveries during the Sep

two and half months supply How
ever, with current operations down to
about 33 per cent of capacity, and the
decline in demand showing signs Of
fattenlng out, producers stocks are
not expected to rise much further.


The industry has recently been sub
jected 10 considerable price cutting.
Prices on the $50 dernier grade viscose
and acetate have dropped from S0.63
to S054 per pound. This, combined
with higher operating and raw ma
terial costs. as well as smaller sales
volumes. has pinched profit margins
severely.

TOXIC, Feb. 26.-Victorious in It's
drst pitched battle with the govern
ment over the drastic general mobili-
nation bill, the Diet subcommittee to
which it was sent for revision avoided
discussion Of 1t In q brief session today.


The 45-member subcommittee con-
vened for 10 minutes and elected a
chairman, then adjourned until Mon
day. It was believed the government
would unlimber It's biggest gun
Premier Prince Fumimaro Konoye-
at the subcommittee's next session.


The premier remained at his SUBJ
urban villa during the general sessions
OF the Diet, when the lower House
howled down government supporters
Of the bitterly controversial measure.


Declared Unconstitutional.


It was criticized as Fascistic and
dictatorial in nature. Members of the
Diet charged it would emasculate the
japanese constitution and rob the peo-
pie Of their basic rights.


Foreign Minister Koki Hirota, War
Minister General Gen Sugiyama, Home
Minister Admiral Nohumasa Suetsuga
and various other hign officials failed
to convince the House 1t was fitting
piece Of legislation. even under the
existing war emergency.


The general mobilization bill would
give the government mandates amount
ing to absolute power over the people
It contains so articles, the first 80 OF
which stipulate government may i'm
press labor for general mobilization
work." appropriate citizens, suppress
newspapers, prohibit the right of as
sembly and suppress freedom Of speech


Each Of these 80 articles begins "ir
time Of war or national emergency. ~
The Diet attacked the phrases am
biguity, charging it would be entirely
subject to the governments interpreta-
ton.


The last 20 articles specify punish
ments for violating the first 30.


Army and Navy Behind Bill.


The army and navy stand solidly be.
hind the bill. Thus, observers see
the basic underlying conflict as per.
haps the last great struggle between
the Diet and the militarists. The Diet
has not offered such resistance in
years.


It approved staggering military bud
gets without dissenting voice and
sanctioned emergency laws for control
OF finance and trade without ques-
ton.


But when it came to the general
mobilization bill. speakers rose to de-
nounce it as high treason against
the state"


Government speakers declared the
bill was necessary purely for China
incident purposes. Cabinet speakers
said they hoped the Diets patriotism
would sanction the bills passage.


Members of the Diet based their
opposition strategy on the conten-
tion that the bill violates article 81
OF the constitution, which directly
names the Emperor and says his pow
ers shall not be superseded.


Cabinet May Resign.


They predicted the government
would pull the bills teeth" and then
resubmit 1t. In case Of an unbreak-
able deadlock, the cabinet may dis
solve the Diet or the cabinet may re-
sign.


Diet dissolution was considered un-
likely. however, since the Diet holds
power over the budget and supple
mentary military estimates have not
yet been passed. Should the Diet be
dissolved, the previous years esti-
mates would remain in effect


The United States, curiously enough,
was dragged into the Diet controversy.
Pro-government newspapers splashed
the American House Committees ap-
proval of measure to give the Presi-
dent wide powers in wartime.


Banner lines said America Passed
General Mobilization Law"


Manchukuo passed a general mobi-
ltzation bill, but news of this action
was given only secondary prominence.
-Four members Of the Diet visited
Home Minister Suetsuga and handed
him a statement demanding protec-
don. They declared their freedom
Of will" had been threatened by the

Special Dispatch to The Star.


MONTREAL, April 25.-The OPEN
ing Of the spring season has found
many Canadian industries working on
reduced schedules, but outstanding in
the contrary direction is the activity
prevailing in the steel. mining and al
lied industries, according to the cur
rent business summary of the Bank
of Montreal.


In general, while business is less
satisfactory than at this period last
year. it is maintaining level better
in substantial degree than that pre-
vailing in the neighboring United
States.


An adverse factor has been the
widespread anxiety about the delicate
international situation, which has
made both business men and investors
in new enterprises hesitant about
undertaking risks. But notwithstand-
ing these factors, during March the
great majority of Canadian industries
did not reduce their scale of oper-
ations from the February level.


The position of heavy industries
has been strengthened by additional
orders for railway equipment and for
airplanes, and in addition there seems
now fair prospect that the British
government will place substantial
orders for aircraft with Canadian
firms.

the social register has just been

Social registerites seldom go to

What will happen when their

Harry K. Thaw, for instance, was

acquitted in the honor" Staying of
Hawaiian accused as her daugh-
ter's ravisher.

Chain Stores Defended


Against Critics.


To the Editor of The Star:


The inevitable Showdown" for chain
stores appears to be coming event
Any great success must face a testing
time; struggle with enemies jealous of
Nctors.


How did our chain stores gain their
1ootlng? In this country no business can
survive without pleasing the public. It
has been amply demonstrated that price
alone Will not build successful busi-
ness. Watch any average food shopper.
Sne may scan the price tags, but she
doesn't always buy the cheapest goods.
An appealing display will make her for
get the budget.


In TACT, display is the secret of chain
store success. Remember the cracker
box cat. the dark, tomblike meat coun-
ter and the jumbled cases of miscel-
laneous junk? Nobody enjoyed buying
because it wasn't a pleasure, an ad-
venture.


How sharply in contrast are the beau
tlful stores we visit today! Well lighted,
they cheer the weary shopper with gay
displays, make her burden easier by
ef1lc1ent methods. The goods are fresher
and new, interesting products line spot
less shelves. Who started all this?
Every American knows the answer
chain stores


Ihe average chain started on a shoe
string, without wealthy backing. A poor
merchant made some improvement,
found it increased his business, made
more improvements, built more stores.
Chain store histories are almost all
similar to this type of growth. American
people chose chains to serve them.
Wnen Americans no longer want chain
stores the business will end Immediately.
Legislators need not be concerned for
fear their constituents cannot get the
type OF stores they want, because the
public holds the purse that pays busi-
ness.


We must conclude that defeated re-
. tallers are at work to regain lost ground
by unfair methods. 1t wouldn't be
American justice to allow them success
IN such venture. Let them present
better service, better advertising, better
display, and they will find that the
"mousetrap" fable still holds true in
this land Of opportunity.


HERNDON P. MURRAY.

For the lover of romance and his

and ready Calamity Jane" and
Poker Alice" whose graves now
stand suitably marked in Mount Mo-
riah Cemetery, once called Boot Hill

ing the stockade that guarded the
handful of whites; the little log hut

mentoes Of those early days, when
the only thing men we're sure of was
that the sun would rise.


Some day great painter may 20

entity: some days great bard may

olence Is to go there.

NEW YORK, Sept. 22.-Rescue

than 200 storm victims from Fire
Island to Bay Shore points. No lives

sons were rushed to hospitals after
reaching safety.

Harbor communities were the most
seriously affected, residents reported,

island. which is located off Long
Island.


Two hundred were rescued by q
Coast Guard ice breaker and several
smaller craft. Many survivors were
reported suffering from exposure and
slight injuries. Homes were swept
into the bay by high winds and waves
lashing at great height over the beach.

mand OF Capt. Gustave Pagels, spent
more than half the night battling its
way across the debris laden bay with
80 storm victims The ferry. Capt.
Pagels said, crashed into four floating
houses during the crossing.


The rescue work continued with
less difhculty today. Approximately
5000 persons reside on Fire Island
during the summer months. The

Dan Cupid with his bow and arrows,

one of these early and irresistably

soon she became Mrs. SaXton, with the

since then Miss Minnie E. Hawke
has been going it alone. Today she
can look back upon a long and sue

many more years of usefulness in this
line of activity, for no one, unfamiliar
with the facts, would suspect that
Miss Hawke had been teaching dancing
for so many years.

James H. Vermilya. one of WASH

who came to Washington about 1870

hvergordon, Rosyth and Scapa Flow

Games May Overlap.

All We know is that our naval

the eastern and western approaches
to the English Channel will be closely

DENVER, May 30 G.N.s),
William Toovey, famous Colorado
stone mason and builder, who
directed construction of the stone
shelter house atop Pixies Peak in
1874, was dead today after q
weeks illness.


Toovey and party Of 10 men
left Colorado Springs in the fall
of 1874 to build the shelter house
for the United States Signal Corps.
Over what is now perhaps the
nations most famed mountain
highway, the men made their way
over a tortuous trail. It showed
nearly every day and the party's
meat spoiled, the men finally be-
ing reduced to boiling bones for
soup.


When the shelter was completed,
the soles had been worn from the
mems shoes and they made their
way down the mountain with
gunnysacks wrapped around their
feet,

watch the races.

Hotel, and final plans for the cor
onation pageant and carnival were
discussed.

number Of pretty girls who have
been named by various governors

Eamon de Valera, American.

prospects of a reciprocal trade
agreement between this country
and the new Fire.

independence will arrive in New
York, May 6, be President Roose-
velt's overnight guest at the
White House May 7, and spend
two days at the legation.

cover Irish-American trade and
political relations, De Valera will
return to New York to open the
Irish exhibit at the World Fair.


Thereafter, the legation indi.
Gated, he will make three weeks
whirlwind tour OF the United
States, probably including Boston,
Chicago, Kansas City, Denver and
San Francisco, cities where, while
a fugitive from British justice, he
raised funds for the independence
cause.


VISIT LONG PLANNED


Irish quarters here said tho
prime minister had been planning
an American visit since 1882, but
had been baked by affairs Of
state from carrying out his plan.


Friends said there was no doubt
the visit has significant political
aspects, but emphasized the pre-.
mier primarily was interested in
renewing friendships with Irish
American leaders who supported
him in the independence fight.

BARCELONA, May "a Q.N.S.)
Nationalist warplaneS raided Bar
celona early today. Casualties wert
not known.


The raiders flew over the city al
a great altitude, rendering anti
aircraft fire Intellectual. Several
bombs struck in the southern part
of the city.


ENDAYE, Franco-Spanish
Border, May "a U.N.S).-Five
nationalist planes heavily bombed
Port Bou, just across the border,
today in a renewal of aerial war.
fare on the Catalan front.


The bombardment of the border
town followed reports that some
of the Government prisoners who
escaped from the Spanish nation
alist prison at Pamplona had
crossed into France.


MASS JAIL BREAK


Advices seeping across the Dor.
der, but not officially confirmed,
indicated between 1000 and 1000
government troops captured dur
ing the civil war escaped from
the San CriStobal prison in a
Mass break.


Refugees who crossed the Pyre-
nees into France said the entire
Navarran countryside was the
scene of a giant nationalist man
hunt for the escaped prisoners.


It also was reported the COVER
nor and captain of the guard OF
the San Cristobal prison were
slain when the prison break took
place.
At Madrid the government ra-
dio station told of another daring
raid in which still more govern
ment prisoners were released from
a nationalist prison camp near
Malaga.


Thirty government troops
landed from small craft near Nal
aga under cover of darkness, &C
cording to this report. and over
powered the garrison at the prison
camp.


FREE 800 PRISONERS

prisoners and sailed with them
to freedom, the broadcast related.

thorities issued communique as

and 387 men were captured, it was
claimed

balan sector were checked. Bar

MARIA, Tex, July 27.-The flood
ing Rio Grande hid today the fate Of
one soldier and marooned his two
companions on tragic attempt to
ride through walled Santa Helena
Canyon on automobile innertubes.


A searching party from Fort d. A.
Russell. from which the men were on
leave, located Sergt. Clyde Ryberg and
Pvt. Clarency Hansen last night The
men were perched on ledge 1000 feet
above the river. but $500 feet below
the canyons rim.


There was no trace. however, Of
Pvt. Harry Buckman. who had joined
IN the week end lark to conquer the
rock-strewn rapids.


Darkness made impossible rescue of
the marooned pair last night, but
food and blankets were dropped to the
ledge, the only break in the otherwise
smooth, steep walls Of the canyon.

The trip had proved that the road to
Tortosa was being defended stubbornly
and steadily and was highly defensible;
that frances forces, trying to march
down the Ebro to the sea, had ad-
vanced only S kilometers in the last
three days; that the morale of the
government troops defending Tortosa
and the Neutrality-suspicious. road was
excellent: that there was no evidence
of any kind Of panic or discourage
ment. but that the troops were very,
very tired.


All the way back toward Tarragona
We passed fresh troops, guns and
trucks loaded with munitions. going
toward the front. Make no mistake
on this, there have been break
throughS, exploited to the full by
mechanical force. Good government
troops have been flanked by enemy
troops pushing through at soft spots
in the line. Important towns and key
towns have been taken. But learning
from an officer just returned from
there that Lerida is now a sort of
no-man's land; with the government
troops still standing solidly outside
OF it across the blown-up bridge, and
seeing the fight being made for Tor
tosa, you see the extent and serious
ness OF the government resistance.


It's not over yet by long shot, and
one thing that has been learned in
this Spanish war is that anything
can happen and that the experts are
always wrong.

NEW YORK. July 16-Commodity
| prices extended this week the rising
| trend of the past two months, moving
up to the highest level since early
April.


Farm products. excepting livestock,
was the only important group of
staples to weaken in face of the gen.
eral advance


The Associated Press weighted index
Of 35 wholesale spot commodity prices
pushed up to 67.74 per cent of the
1926 average from 6756 last week and
compared with 81 so a year ago.
Rising briskly early in the week, the
list reacted moderately toward the
end.


Livestock again set the pace. Jump
ing to the highest point since last De-
cember, % per cent above the years
low established during the first week
of May.


Present Supplies Light.
Buoyancy in this category largely
resulted, commodity men said. from
the relatively strong demand in pri-
mary markets and the fact present
supplies are light. Hogs and cattle
shared the upturn, lamb dipping
slightly


Other products of the farm, how
ever. did not fare so well. The recent
Government crop report was followed
by sharp decline in wheat approx
lmately 6 cents bushel. Oats, rye
and cotton also were depressed. while
corn managed small gain.


The slump in wheat resulted in
large measure from pressure of the
generous harvest-second largest on
record-and in some respects from un-
favorable trade reaction to the setting
OF crop loan figures.


industrial raw materials continued
the advancing pace of recent weeks
Non-ferrous metals, however, which
have been the fastest rising group
since mid-June, were inactive and
unchanged. Tin alone moved, gaining
slightly.

pentine and bituminous coal. Rub
per- on the other hand, weakened
after the sensational upswing of the
past month.

and silk moving up.

although most closed behind plus
signs. Sugar, coffee, -four and lard

Frontier, March 81 (Pl.-Insurgent
Generalissimo Franco today aimed
twin thrusts toward. the Mediterra-
mean and deadly severance of gov
ernment Spain.


The central army worked it's way
through the suburbs of Lerida, ancient
city and fortress, 80 miles from Bar
celona and but As miles from the
coastal city of Tarragona.


Gan Associated Press dispatch
from Barcelona reported five in
surgent planes had dropped 80
bombs on nearby Mataro, destroyed
several houses, killed S persons and
wounded 20 today. The planes
turned toward Barcelona, not
bombed in II days, but sped to sea
when government fighters pursued)
The right wing, AZ miles to the
south, menaced Gandesa, an outpost
also on the road to Carragona. This
force already had crossed the Algas
River, miles west of Gandesa, and
was slightly closer to the coast than
the army investing Lerida.


Insurgents were attempting to sur
round and isolate the government gar
rison in Lerida, the castle that defends
the Serge River Valley, which has
been described as the gateway" to
Barcelona.


Can Associated Press dispatch
from Tarbes, France, declared 1000
Spanish government militiamen,
cut off from their base by new
irsurgent advance east of Jaca,
escaped across the Pyrenees today
into the tiny French mountain
hamlet Of Hospice de France.


(They surrendered their rifles
and arms without resistance, and
said q thousand others were on
their way to France from the
Pyrenees sector.


mobile guardsmen rushed to the
town at the call of the hamlet's
Mayor and found the weary, hungry
soldiers stumbling down mountain
trails from the mountain heights.)


Insurgents predicted the quick
fall of Lerida and moved up truckloads

pectation of its occupation.

to the east, from Balaguer to Borjas
Blancas.

Rising Sun were reported flying from
government buildings tonight in
| Suchow as japanese troops fought

nants of Chinese forces to complete
| occupation of the city.


japanese military quarters, however,
declined to say that the city. long re-

central front resistance, had been cap

Correspondents of Domei. japanese
news agency. reported from Suchow
that it was virtually captured" adding
that an airdrome on the outskirts had
been occupied and that japanese war
planes were landing there. Large sec
tions of the city were in flames.


(At HonkoW a Chinese military


spokesman belittled the japanese


reports. asserting that the Hankow


headquarters had been informed by


telephone from Suchow that the


city was still in Chinese hands.)


Fierce Fighting Near TsaOchow.


The japanese reported fierce en-
gagement with Chinese forces near
Tsaochow, 130 miles northwest Of
Suchow, in which 700 Chinese were
killed The survivors fed south
toward the Lunghai Railway, the
strategic communications line which
runs west through Suchow into Gen.
tral China.


japanese aviators said Suchow,
viewed from the air, was a blob Of
smoke creased by jagged flames.


They said naval planes bombing
from low altitude scored a direct hit
on what apparently was the main mu-
nitions storehouse, sending flames and
smoke hundreds Of feet into the air.


Another tremendous fire, also ap-
parently from powder magazine, was
reported in the southeastern section
of the city.


Fighting in Southern City.


All the city except the southern
part, where fighting continued, was
said by the Japanese to have been oc-
cupied within few hours after they
stormed the wall and poured into the
vital Central China rail junction.


Severe fighting was reported spread
ing to the south suburbs, where the
Chinese dare to die" units were
counter tacking in an effort to en-
able the main Chinese forces to with
draw southwark and escape annihila-
ton.


Japanese troops advancing north
ward along the Tentsin-Pukow Rail-
way still were As miles south of
Suchow, leaving wide gap through
which the Chinese might escape.


Strikes At Langhai.


Meanwhile, the fast-moving jap
anese war machine struck at other
points along the Lunghai in an effort
to gain complete possession Of this
life line" across Central China and
prepare for the big drive on Hankow.
the provisional capital.


Gen. Count Juichi Terauchi, COM
mander Of Japan's North China
Armies, watched the desperate strug-
gle for strategic Suchow from an air
plane over the city, according to

No Chinese planes took to the air,
and anti-aircraft batteries had been
silenced.

Tomorrow is the Chinese New Year
under the old lunar calendar-a day
that in years gone by saw joyous cele-
bration in Washington's Chinese quar-
ter. but with their native land she'll
shocked and war-torn. members of
the colony are planning a compara-
lively quiet celebration.


Where in previous years there was
much visiting and renewing old friend
ships with wishes for prosperous
new year over glass of wine. tomor-
row will be quiet exchanges of hopes
for more peaceful days in their home
land.


Although the Chinese government
has officially adopted the solar calen-
dar Of the Western world, the older
Chinese generation still reckons time
by the lunar system. using the moon
and the tides as the basis for calcu-
lation.


During the reigns of emperors each
new ruler gave name to his tenure
of office on ascending the throne and
years were dated from his ascension.
The year beginning tomorrow will be
known as the twenty-seventh year of
the republic, which was established
In 1911, after the revolution.

the coaches eyed these youngsters with
particular hope. Two ends, Dan Bates
and Sam Babich. as well as Batson and
Sartore are counted on for steady
service.


With last years three top ends, Pete
Yurwitz, Lloyd Berry and Tippy Hout,
all gone the way of June graduation,
Bates and Babich may step right into
the regular lineup if they come up to
expectations Eberle and Bob Faris,
a fine pass receiver but too small for

wingmen at hand, so Reinhart has
reason to keep an eye on the flank
situation


Problem at Center.


He also has a problem at center
which must be filled primarily with
sophomore material. Tim Stapleton
and Allen Hallberg, last years centers,
are gone. Only Jones, who was moved

in the spring, has had varsity expert

From the sophs, then. must come
the reserve corps and Reinhart will

BUDAPEST, Oct. 4-Numerous war
veterans more than As years old had
orders to report to the nearest army
recruiting station today as the Hun
garian government pressed dts claims
to Hungarian minority territories OF
CzechoSlovakia.


The requisition Of certain raw ma
terials and orders prohibiting the ex-
ports Of metals, textiles, chemicles and
leather were made known today, ap-
parent indications that Hungary was
preparing for all eventualities.


While the foreign Office awaited
Prague's answer to a note in which
the immediate beginning of negotia-
tions for the return Of Hungarian ter
ritories was asked, cabinet meeting
was called for this afternoon to de-
eide what measures should be taken
should Czechoslovakia refuse to COM
ply with Hungarian demands.


Terror" Declared Increasing.


Newspaper reports of increased
Czech terror" angered Hungarians
meanwhile. Mass meetings in various
parts Of Hungary demanded immediate
occupation of Czechoslovak territory
inhabited by 800, 1000 Hungarians.


The government handed Czecho-
slovakia a new note last night asking
negotiations at once and requesting
guarantees that the discussions would
be conducted in "the right at
mosphere" to assure quick solution.


Some newspapers declared Czecho-
slovak Legionnaires plundered and
burned numerous Magyar-inhabited
villages in Southern Czechoslovakia.


(The reports lacked confirmation
from other sources)


Dispatches from Bratislava said
eight Hungarian-speaking recruits
were shot there for insubordination.


Food Seized BY Army.


Travellers reaching Budapest from
the Hungarian minority district of
Komorom, near the Danube, said some
suffering was experienced by farmers
and worker% there, chiefly because
massing OF troops along the border re-
suited in inadequate food distribution
1t was said potatoes and grain were
largely requisitioned. for the army.


The travellers said they saw no indi-
cation that the Czechoslovak army in
tended to leave these so-called purely
Hungarian districts, as the Hungarian
government demanded, "uncondition-
ally and Immediately"


Reports from the Hungarian side of
the Danube said Czechoslovak troops
had reinforced barbed wire lines along
the border and that additional war
equipment was being brought up
Concrete walls were reported being
built as protection against tanks on
highways connecting Czechoslovakia
and Hungary.


Freedom Promised Soon.


Premier Bella 1mredi and other
cabinet members assured the nation
that Hungarian minorities would soon
be free from the Czech yoke"


The foreign Office press chief said
no indication had come from Prague
as to when minority negotia tons would
start, but he added that the govern
ment was convinced Prague would
agree to begin the discussions within
two or three days.


A foreign Office map showing loca-
tions of Magyars in Slovak territory
in 1910 indicated some 5000 square
miles were populated then by Magyars.

The Washington tourney for the

usually operate from small junks, have
raided several Chinese fishing towns along

women.

second singles place. Riggs outranks
the others nationally. but the choice
probab bly, will be made on the showing

ampton, Rye and Newport.


Il haven't mapped out any definite
campaign to win place on the Davis
Cup team" said Riggs, but. Of course,
that is the greatest ambition of my
life"

trouble beating young Carleton Rood
in straight sets. While Riggs was
paired today with Gerard Podesta,
captain-elect of the Princeton Varsity,

year-old Frank Guernsey, national
intercollegiate titleholder.


Guernsey Eager for Match.


Guernsey. 5-foot-4 dynamo, whose
game has been compared with that of

breezed through two early opponents
with ease and expressed no fear for
the highly rated Parker.


I've always wanted to meet him"

The famous Harris Tweeds came in
to being through an accident Of ma
ture. The freezing winds which swept
across the barren islands Of the Outer
Hebrides, of the coast Of Scotland,
made 1t imperative that the natives
have warm windproof. weather-proof
garments. With nowhere else to turn,
the women of the islands took advan-
tage of the unusually thick fleece
which was the winter coat Of their
sheep, and from 1t they wove for their
men the first crude Harris tweeds
Because they had nothing but the
natural vegetable dyes made from
lichens and crottle, and nowhere to
steep their wool except over peat fires,
Harris tweed has always been charac-
terized by peaty outdoor odor. These
tweeds had been worn in the Outer
Hebrides for many years before the
fashion centers Of the world discovered
them and elevated them to the front
rank Of sports fashions.

LONDON, Aug. 27.-A freak acci-
dent wrecked Great Britains new
transatlantic airliner the Albatross.
late today at the conclusion of a final
test flight.


The winged four-engined mono
plane broke in two upon landing at
Hatfield Airdrome. The plane settled
down with its nose pointing skyward.
its tail, level with the ground, split off
Just behind the wing like bird with
broken back. No one was injured.


The Albatross. Britain's fastest air.
liner, with sister plane nearing cem-
pletion. was scheduled to start trans
Atlantic service in September.


Capt. Godfrey de Havlland. chief
test pilot for the De Havilland Aircraft
Co, and an observer scrambled
through the emergency door unhurt
after the crash. Officials of the COM
pany were unable to explain the cause
of the accident and declined to dis
close what would be done with the
uncompleted sister ship and others
going into production.


The flight was "full-load" test de-
signed to measure the planes capabil-
tiles with the equivalent of % paSsen-
gers flying more than 200 miles an
hour with its four 00-horsepower en-
glnes wide open.

The colonists are IL youths from

Seven of the boys are on Canton

Except for several carpenters vino

Solution Seen Possible.


A State Department official, after

solution of the ownership problem
could be reached. The note was said

Interior Department officials COM
municated yesterday by radio with

B. Black, who headed the occupation
expedition.


In lieu of information to the con-
trary, they assumed a New Zealand
expedition which visited the islands
last May had departed and that two
American flags deposited on Canton
at the same time by the Nationa,
Geographic Society's eclipse expedi-
ton were still there.


Following London dispatches which
mentioned the possibility of a Brit.
ish proposal for Joint control ovel
the islands, officials studied prece-
dents for such an action.


Interest in New Hebrides.


They were particularly interested
IN the case of the New Hebrides
Islands, which might be suggested by
the British as an example.


The New Hebrides, lying 500 miles
west of the Fiji Islands, have beer
operated efficiently under joint Anglo.
French control since 1906


The fact that Canton and Ender-
bury Islands may be used for com.
mercial aviation between the United
States and British dominions lent
added weight to the possibility of Joint
control

Tossing titfully in fever that
comes one day, but always vanisheS
the next, Maxine has slept through
three Christmas holidays, victim
of encephalitis lethargica sleeping
sickness.


They call her the sleeping BEAU
ty" of ST. Francis Hospital. where
other little patients clapped hands
excitedly today in expectation of
Santa's annual visit.


Physicians said they had no hope
the 5-year-old child would awaken
for this Yule holiday. the fourth
that has passed her by. They fear
she may never recover. although
Maxine has gained weight and
stature during more than three
years in the hospital. and she has
escaped the usual children's dis
eases. She has never had cold

liquid diet she has received since
entering ST. Francis in 1885. Except
for the occasional rise in tempera-

within "a hours, her condition re-
mains unchanged from month to
month.


For Maxine's mother this will be
another Christmas of waiting for
the day when the child will return
to the home at nearby Fairview to
join her two brothers and sister.
Despite the word of physicians, the
mother has never lost hope this
would come about.

24.-Special details of State and
Prince Georges County police were

crowd of racing fans at the open

boro Fairgrounds.


For the first time this year will
see the races and the fair held as
separate events, John Boyle, secre-
tary of the Maryland Agriculture
Fair Association, announced today.


A reported $75, 900 worth of i'm
provements to the grounds and
the race course are responsible for
the split card, Boyle explained,
since the several additions to the
stables and seating accommoda-
tions have limited the space avail
able for fair purposes. The fair
proper will open october 13 and
continue through the fifteenth.


Also listed among the improve
ments to Marlboro's half-mile
track will be the appearance for

ELMONT, N. Y, Jan. 13 Q.N.SO &.
The Staying of 59-year-old Mrs.
Lenida Waite and 19-year-old Jean
Schuelain without apparent mo-
tive, occupied attention of New
York's homicide experts today.


Sometime between 4 and 5
o'clock yesterday afternoon,
vicious killer literally blasted the
brains out of the woman and her
young visitor with a gun which
left quarter-inch holes in the
skulls.


At 5 o'clock, George Waite, 26,
the widows son, arrived home,
he told police, and sat downstairs
for two hurs before looking for his
mother.


QUARREL HINTED


Two circumstances pointed to-
early solution of the crime and the
cause, authorities said. One was
that the WaiteS' police dog which
barks If a stranger even passes
the house was silent yesterday
The other was that loud voices,
indicating a quarrel, were hard
coming from the house during the
afternoon.


Mrs. Waite apparently was the
intended victim. the Schuelain
girl an incidental victim. The
fact that she was still wearing
hel coat when hel body was found
tieG. to chair indicated that she
walked IN on the murder scene
ano was slain to silence her.


Police said Mrs. Waite had no
money, nothing to steal, indicat.
Ing the motive was not robbery
On the other hand. they added,
she led a retired life and could
hardly nave incurred an enemy
among her small circle Of friends
who would be so bitter as to kill
her, then add another murder to
tie evil deed.


FINDS HER DEAD


On arriving home, Waite said,
he called to his mother and get
tirE no answer through she had
gone out. possibly to the Schuelain
home. He went there but she
wasn't there and neither was
Jean.


He returned bone and occupied
himself with his newspaper until
almost Z o'clock. Then Mrs. Bertha
Peckham, a cousin who boarded
with the Waites. arrived. She
asked at once where Mrs. Waite
vas. George guessed she was
'fout."


When the police arrived, thev
started search of the upstairs
rooms and found Miss Schuelain's
body. Both women had been
gagged with silk stockings, bound
and shot.

The Nations business receded last
| week.


Once more the steel industry ac-
celerated operations, but demand was
slow in most sectors. Moderate losses
were posted for electricity output, car
loadings and automobile production.
Retail trade, for the most part,
slipped back into slower tempo" the
Commerce Department said in its sur
vey of SO cities.


There was corresponding easing
on in wholesale activities. While
orlgnt spots were apparent here and
tnere, the reports in the main pre-
sented a rather unhappy chronicle
OF the current business picture, with
evidences of growing UNEMPLOYMENT
being one of the distressing factors"
Inc Associated Press index of in
dustrlal activity declined to 1872 from
1874 the previous week.


Steel Operations Higher.


The steel industry stepped up opera
tions to 327 per cent capacity from
29.S the previous week. the American
Iron and Steel Institute estimated.
IN the corresponding week last year
tne rate was 77.9 per cent.


Except for railroad buying and some
building and construction Jobs Of fair
Size. current orders are small, Iron
Age reported.


The motor industry, normally
heavy consumer of steel, has been
taxing but a fraction of the amount
1t bought at this time last year. Busi-
ness expected a week ago from two
important makers failed to material
ize, steel circles reported.


The stock market-traditional bar
ometer of the Nations business hopes
and fears-went into a slump. Wall
street analysts said the largest batch
OF selling orders followed the state
ment Of President Roosevelt that in
oustrlal prices should be cut and
wages maintained in order to sluice
new activity into business channels.


Trade Situation Spotty.


Bonds were irregularly lower. High
priced railroad bonds yielded with
liens in the medium and low-price
brackets. Most important raw ma
terials gave better account of them
selves than securities.


Reports to the Commerce DEPART
ment on business conditions follow:
New York department stores had sales
a little under a year ago Boston.s
retail turnover was about even with a
year ago. Philadelphia and Cleveland
madesa brighter showing.


Retail losses were noted by Chicago.
St. Louis. Kansas City. San Fran
cisco, Detroit, Pittsburgh, Milwaukee
and Omaha, but trade improvement
was reported in Dallas, Seattle, New
Orleans and Atlanta.


Motor Output Declines.


Steel men. attempting to gauge the
outlook, found the motor industry
provided little cheer. In the week
just closed, output dropped to 59,365
units from 65,418 the week before
and compared with 76,62O in the like
1897 week, Wards Automotive Re-
ports said. The survey added indi-
cations were the general trend would
be somewhat lower for the coming
weeks. 1t estimated February pro-
duction at about 100000. This would
be downswing of about IS per cent
from the like month a year ago.


In the week ended January %
freight carloadings totaled 57O,333
cars, decline of l.8 per cent from
the previous week, the Association of
American Railroads reported. This
was 14.3 per cent under the corre-
spending period last year. Lower ship
ments Of coal and miscellaneous
freight helped pull the total down.


Dividends Cut or Passed.


Production of electricity totaled
2,l08,96 900 kilowatt hours in the
week ended January %, the Edison
Electric Institute reported This was
0.3 of per cent under the previous
week. decline which experts termed
less than usual at this season. Out
put was 66 per cent off from the cor.
responding week of 1887.


Observers scanning the national
business scene found most indicators
tilted lower. For the eleventh con-
secutive week bank clearings dipped
in leading cities, Dun g. Bradstreet
said. Cash money in circulation. a
measure Of the pulse of trade. was
down. Several industrial companies
either cut or omitted dividends.

The bodies of three more of the H.

rain squall, within view of maneuver-

The 11-P-3 fell in flames. The IL

den downdraft. They were cruising
at about 140 miles an hour, close
above four battleships and 20 de-
stroyers.


Searchlights suddenly Illuminated
the scene and warship launches put

CERBERE, France, May 27.-Anti-
aircraft guns were wheeled into posi-
ton today to protect this frontier
town from repetition Of last nights
air attack


The Mayor of Cerbere had tele-
graphed Premier Daladier that The
population protests against insufficient
measures taken to protect it against
Italo- German aviation"


Reassured by arrival of anti-aircraft
batteries, the inhabitants of Cerbere
came out of hiding. Many of the
1000 residents had huddled in under
ground refugees while 8 warplanes
bombarded Cerberes railway terminal.


The planes were identified unom-
cially as Spanish insurgent.


Destroyers Are Sent.


From Paris Navy Minister Cesar
Campinchi ordered destroyers Of the
Mediterranean feet to cruise of Ger
bere to help repel any new attack.


"a foreign Office spokesman said
a thorough" investigation of the
bombing had been ordered and that
France would protest vigorously
when the nationality of the bomb
ers was determined)


Village authorities rushed the cltl-
zens to safety last night in the rail-
road tunnel several hundred yards
long that connects Cerebere with the
neighboring Spanish town, Port Bou.


Not a single bomb, however, struck
Port Bou, although for the 41st time
it was insurgent aviators' objective.


Three Hurt by Glass.


Three persons here were wounded
by flying glass. Windows and door
ways of the international railway sta
ton were shattered, three houses
were destroyed and 1 Alton mail car
was blasted from the tracks.


The squadron dropped Is bombs
before retreating under fire of Spanish
government anti-aircraft batteries.
French searchlights silhouetted the
planes, but French guns did not fire.


French border officials doubted that
the rain of bombs on French territory
was anything but tragic error"
but some pointed out that the attack
was concentrated about the clearly
marked railroad station, which in
surgents had claimed to be the source
of much equipment for government
troops.


Cerbere is the control point of the
principal railway linking France and
government SpainS


No French action was expected until
after officials had completed an in
vestigation.


Attack From North.


Border observers were puzzled that
the attack came from the north. The
planes were said to have flown down
the French Coast from the direction
of Banyuls- -sur-Mer, about 4 miles
above Cerbere. The ships departed
in the direction Of the insurgent
air base in the Balearic Islands.


Across the Pyrenees frontier. mean
while, the government increased its
efforts to crack lines the insurgents
have established on the western fringeS
of Catalonia.


Border dispatches said the heaviest
fighting was going on between the
Mango Range north of Llavorsi and
the Monsech Range south of Tremp.
Cutting the road between Tremp and
Balaguer to the south was said to
have endangered insurgent positions,
as there was no way of bringing up
reinforcements.

Y VIRGINIA Is big state and 1t
~ offers many sights for the


" traveller. perhaps the most un-


usual and the least exploited
OF all being her Indian Reservations.
Yes. Indian Reservations in Virginia!
There are two of them, only few
miles apart, and only l25 miles from
Washington. The larger contains the
Pamunkey tribe. the other, the
Mattaponi.


Withir . three-hour drive of WASH
ington these Indians, the direct des-
cendants Of the two leading tribes
Of Powhatan's Confederacy, live under
their old tribal laws. on land that
has never been owned by white men.
Their reservations are different from
any others in the country. The vir-
ginia Indians are not wards Of the
government; they rule and support
themselves. They are free and inde-
pendent Of the state in which they
are located. Other reservations, even
the immense Navajo and Hopi tracts
in Arizona. are governed by state
laws, but only Federal statutes cover
the Virginia Indians.


The Pamunkeys make their own
game and fish laws, the chief and
council decide all matters of state,
both legislative and juridical Every
year they travel to Richmond to renew
the treaty Of 1646 which guarantees
their freedom and independence on
their reservation. In return for Ger
tain wild game deer, several furs,
q fox-the governors of Virginia have
every year since 1916 acknowledge
the autonomy Of the Pamunkeys.


These Inians, = dignified people
are Of course proud of their present
liberty, but prouder still OF their past
glory. King Powhatan. whose power
full Confederation included 80 tribes
with lands ranging from the Atlantic
seacoast to the Blue Ridge, was a Pa
munkey. His people, who once held
the thread Of life and death over the
few pale faces" IN their midst, have
written . sorry later history for them
selves. The story of the ten lost
tribes Of Lsreal Is magnified threefold,
for of the 81 tribes under Powhatan,
only two are left rs tribal organisa-
tions. The two, of course, are the
Pamunkey and the Mattaponi (pro-
nounced Matta-p'n-eye).


PAMUNKEY history was closely in


terwoven with that of John Smith
and his band of Englishmen. The
story Of Pocahontas, the Chiefs
daughter, and John Smith is a favor
ite with the Indian as well as the
white man. The following is the
Indian story Of the event, translated
from sign language. 1t is . MASTER
piece OF understatement: Indians,
while hunting. discover white men
standing in shallow water. Indians
agree to kill white men at Chiefs
seat Indian maiden lPocahontas)
disagrees with Indian men and makes
for no harm to white men, but good
wishes"

controversy with Reich officials

Banned for a week, Der Sitter
mer reappeared today with glar-
ing anti-Jewish headlines and
gross pictorial onslaughts against
Jews in Hollywood and elsewhere.


CITY PLACARDED


To signalize his triumph, Strei-
cher flooded Berlin with five-foot
high posters.


When his paper was banned
for running a series Of special
issues demanding the death pen
atty for Aryans incurring the
racial disgrace" Of marrying
Jews, reports arose that the gov
ernment was planning to let up in
its anti-Semitic campaign.





Some sort Of face-saving agree
ment was reached, however. The
editor and a few members of his
staff were dismissed, but Streicher
was allowed to remain and ap-
parently given official approval Of
his editorial activities.


OLD TACTICS REVIVED


Today's edition carried another
headline with the words death
penalty" and racial disgrace"
and on the front page was a two
column picture Of young Holly
wood actress with her director
and producer. The caption be-
meath it, painting the alleged
fate Of innocent girls at the hands
Of Jews, defies respectable trans
lation.


The ban on Streicher's paper
lasted only five days after he met
and talked things over with Hit
ler.

ZARAGOZA. April Insurgent
commanders announced today they
had seized the positions dominating
Lerida, key city in northeastern
Spain and that occupation of the
provincial capital awaited only a
cleanup of the Segre River Valley.


Battling with tanks and machine
guns Though the olive groves and
hills about Lerida. troops commanded
by Gen. Juan Vague continued their
ehcircling movement of the historic
citadel and expected the last ma jor
barrier to Barcelona and the Mediter-
ranean Coast soon would fall. Gov
ernmenG forces. however, had pre-
pared a new defensive line 10 miles
to the East, and resisted savagely
every step.


Meanwhile. the flight to France of
defeated government militia continued
as the spreading insurgent offensive
threatened to isolate Catalonia, the
governments major stronghold.


$50 An Hour.


Refugees from the war front were
arriving at the rate of about $50 an
hour at Bagneres de Luchon, on the
frontier.


One thousand troops and 1000
civilians fled yesterday and French
border officials shifted them to camps
in frontier towns. The soldiers were
disarmed.


tIn Barcelona, the Catalan trade


unions appealed for 100000 volun-


teers to fight the rebels.)


Insurgents said they found copy
OF an order from the government COM
mand directing the officers to keep
their front lines from retreating
under the penalty of death if neces-
sary for fleeing troops.


Government losses in the hard
fought conflict were declared to be
unusually heavy.


Rebels Win in North.


Insurgents reported the capture Of
large number of prisoners in the
Lerida sector. including the chief of
the sanitary corps of the Eel Camp
esino' brigade and a Lister brigade
major, Carmelo Martinez of Madrid.


The insurgent drive was pushing up
along the Pyrenees frontier and down
toward the Mediterranean coastal
plain to cut Catalan communications
with the rest of government Spain
Barcelona and Madrid.


In the north, Insurgent Gen.
frances Spanish troops occupied
Graus, 81 miles over the French bor-
der, and pursued the governments S
fleeing militia up the Esera River gap
into the mountains. ,


1t was believed Binefar, on the road
running southeast from Barbastro to
Lerida. had been evacuated by the
government


Italians Win.


On the southern sector Gen. Garcia
Vallnos Italians and Navarrese Divi-
sion and Col. Jose Monasterio's cavalry
broke the enemy's resistance at
Nonaspe. 10 miles east of the battle
field of Caspe, and advanced through
the Matarrana River Valley into the
Catalan Province of Tarragona, inflict-
ing heavy losses on the enemy and
seizing large stores.


The Italian Black Arrow column
captured an entire enemy battalion, it
reported, including 10 English soldiers
with their captain.


Here the insurgents were barely 40
miles from the coast.


French Resort Packed.


BAGNERES DE LUCHON, France.
April P.-Thousands of Spanish
military and civilian refugees fleeing
before the great insurgent drive
through Northeastern Spain today
packed this French mountain resort
after days of terrible hardships in the
Pyranees.


Through deep SHOWS the refugees
plodded toward a haven in friendly
France, but many of their compan-
ions already had met death in plunges
into snow-filled canyons.


French frontier guards found the
stiffened bodies of others where they
had dropped from exhaustion in the
snowbanks. Bodies lay on rocky
slopes and ridges. Some had literally
fallen over the border into France and
to their deaths.


The refugees arrived in desperate
need of food and shelter. Here
mothers and children were given first
places in hastily erected shelters and
private homes, were fed hot meals and
given warm covers. But all were
warned their respite in France would
be brief.

Possibility that the Federal Gov
ernment may force State and local
officials to rid all the streams OF
the nation of pollution is being
studied today.


This development came to light
yesterday at a press conference
held by Secretary of the Interior
Harold L. Ickes. Asked if the Fed
eral Government could compel
backward States and cities to
clean up their rivers under the
Constitution. the Secretary said:


Wen have our lawyers study
the law and see just what can
be done"


POWERS NEGLECTED


Constitutional clauses giving the
Federal Government exclusive
jurisdiction over navigable streams
and the general welfare clause are
deemed the ones directly bearing
on the situation.


President Roosevelt and Secre-
tary Ickes are both known to feel
that States and municipalities
have failed to exercise to the full
extent police powers granted them
to rid streams of domestic sewage
and industrial waste.


PWA GRANTS MADE


Through PWA grants already
made and applications for further
financial aid filed by officials of
various communities, the Potomac
and many tributary streams are to
be rid of pollution.


However, visits to towns along
the Potomac and feeder" streams
convinced reporters that office
holders in some communities are
inclined to ignore the pollution
problem.

The slender. often twisted but withal

Identify this tree when bare.


The bark Is dark brown, slightly
broken into burrows. which divide into
thick, irregular plates. Sometimes you
can see the smooth, satiny bark that
covers the younger limbs.


Early in April the slender, brown
buds. some one-fourth inch in length,
show evidence of having awakened
from the long winters sleep. BY the
latter part of April the flowers, both
staminate and pistillate, arrive be-
fore the procession of the leaves. The
male leaves are in catkins 3 to 4
inches long, Of a purplish yellow. The
female blossoms are erect, one-half
10 l inch long; the bracts are hairy
and ovate.


Hordes Of insects may b. h.srd
humming over the cherry birch es you
stand beneath the tree. The winds
have sifted pounds Of golden pollen
from the male flowers to the waiting
female flowers nearby. Thus IS as
sured the June crop of fruit which
you will later see, the erect little cones
with broad scales and three distinct,
rounded lobes. The nut children un-
der these scales have narrow wings
which taper at the base. When they
are ready to 60 with the wind, the
cone scales release them and away

ROME, April 30.-A passenger plane
bound from Tirana. Albania, to Rome,

near Formia. Italy

had crashed. but a reliable source
said it was certain that disaster had
overtaken the craft, which was equip

The airline Office spokesman said
there was nothing to say before to-
morrow morning."


One report, reaching Rome from
Tirana, said the plane carried passen-
gers returning to Italy from the we'd
ding of King Zog and Queen Geraldine
of Albania.


The plane. carrying its full load of

ern Italy. this morning after an un-
eventful flight across the Adriatic Sea
from Tirana. 1t had been due in

feet mirror. The trees themselves
are draped in graceful swaying
Spanish moss.

NEW YORK, Jan. 8.-Commodity
prices rallied in the opening week Of
1888, chalking up the biggest gains
since last September under the leader
ship of non-ferrous metals and farm
products.


A few industrial staples were lower.
however, and live stock slumped to the
lowest level since early in 1885.


The Associated Press weighted index
of IS important wholesale commodity
prices rose to 74.14 per cent of the
1925 average from 1885 last week, and
compared with 90.16 year ago.


The smart upturn in stock prices
during the week provided the cue for
some of the more speculative staples.
The sharpness of the rebound from
the previous weeks low point stemmed
largely from spurts in the latter group.


Wheat Takes Lead.


The grains. with wheat far out in
front, responded to reports competitive
foreign crops were faring poorly. Oats
and rye pushed ahead, while corn
dipped moderately. Cotton picked up
as the trade viewed nearby consump-
ton prospects favorably, although
reserving decision on the ultimate ef-
fects on prices of the largest crop ever
harvested.


Tin, lead and copper were marked
up fractionally with buying again ap-
pearing in the market The buyers
strike, evident since last summer, was
apparently set aside by pressure of de-
pleted inventories.


Steel scrap, buoyant in previous
weeks, fell back slightly as manufac-
turer demand spent itself. Rubber
ard burlap also weakened in the face
OF reduced inquiries. Bituminous coal
and turpentine, however, were up
slightly.


Food Prices Climb.


Food climbed as rush of buying

By the Associated Press.


Finding of four more bodies in the
Dance township, Ontario, forest fire
area brought to 21 today the known
dead from the blazes that swept the
Minnesota Canadian border region
Monday. Several others were missing,
including six members of the Stone
family.


The latest victims accounted for
were Mr. and Mrs Sam Fyle, age 81
and 10, respectively: an 18month-old
son Donald, and Mabel Larson, 12-
year-old sister of Mrs Fyle.


Their burned home was in the area,
so miles northwest Of Fort Frances,
Ontario, where at least IA others per-
ished.


Rescuers found the four bodies along
a trail where they had been trapped.


Provincial police learned Mrs. Fyle,
an expectant mother, had been stay
ing at her parents cabin, some dis
tance from the Fyle place When the
fires threatened Monday she left with
her small boy and sister to warn
her husband, who was cutting pulp
wood. They apparently reached Mr.
Fyle and all died in vain attempt
to flee the sweeping flames. Her
mothers home did not burn.


Also missing was family named
Stone which lived in Kingsford Town
ship which. like Dance Township. was
swept by the roaring fire. The Stone
family included the parents and four
children. Police said it may be days
before fate of all residents of the area
is learned.


Thousands Patrol Area.


Airplanes, National Guard trucks
and thousands of men patroled the
fre-ravaged area.


Although scattered showers and lower
temperatures had greatly improved
conditions, authorities said, grimy,
weary fire fighters were watching
blazes from Warroad, Mimi, eastward
on both sides of the border to prevent
new outbreaks of the fires.


Several hundred settlers from the
ontario Ganger zones were Drought
into Fort Frances last night, and a
crew of 500 men remained to fight the
fires. The weather was clear and there
was little wind today.


Vic Lofgren, forest ranger at Little
Fork, Mimi, said he had about 1900
men guarding the smouldering fires
in the International Falls district.


Minnesotas adjutant general, Ell
lard A. Walsh, in st. Paul, ordered q
National Guard airplane and several
trucks and ambulances to the danger
zone to aid in fighting the fires and
evacuating settlers. Ontario police and
forestry officials ordered all residents
out of the Dance township area and
rushed in crews of fire fighters.

DELAVAN, ILL.,. March 9 IN.S0
The question of whether beauteous
Mrs. Collision Crabb was a murder
victim instead of a suicide was
officially raised for the first time
here today.


Coroner Nelson Wright brought
the matter into the open in ques-
tioning James Crabb. husband of
the 19-year-old bride of five weeks,
when he asked bluntly:


Would it have been possible
for someone to kill your wife?"


FURTHER INQUIRY


Young Crabb, who said he was
in the bathroom early last Tues
day when his wife was shot, an.
swered:


Il wouldn't know about that"


With his testimony, the coroner
adjourned the inquest until Satur-
day at the request of authorities
for more time to investigate the
mysterious shooting.


Earlier in the hearing, other
members of the Crabb family said
that while waiting for doctor
they had left the fatally wounded
girl alone and did not know
exactly when she died.


QUARREL ADMITTED


Willis w. Crabb, wealthy preSi-
dent of the Teazewell National
Bank, in whose home his son and
daughter-in-law were living, ad-
mitted quarreling with the young
couple when they came in after
party and disturbed his sleep.


Officers testified they had found
the gun, an old frontier model
belonging to young Crabb, jammed
between the mattress and the head
of the bedStead with the butt
barely visible. There were no
fingerprints on the weapon, a po-
lice expert asserted.

Martha Tobin dug her ski pole deeper into
the snowdrift and stood there, looking across
the fifty yard eternity at Quen. She was trying
to memorize the lean, easy grace of his pose the
lift of his dark head, before he was shut from
sight by the red woolens, the blue gabardines,
the stocking caps, the peaked Alpine caps and
the fur parkas of the twenty other skiers who
smged forward in a jocular wave around -
Quen and Suzanne.


After a decent interval of stretching her
smile, Martha slipped away. There was ridge
yonder and beyond it, small, lonely valley
laced with blue shadows and shuttered with
trees like crystal decorations in Christmas
window.


Her skis took her lightly down the slope and
for the first time she treasured their eager obedi
ence. She was not good skier; plain poor,
according to Quen. But Quen never suspected
the black fear that rode down every steep slide
partner because Quen was at her other elbow.
But now ..


The valley was deserted; unmarked except
for her own tracks from that morning where she
had worked alone at the head of the valley
patiently perfecting her Telenark turns. For
Quen's sake. The ski tracks were punctuated
by unpfetty muddles of snow like beads along
string. This morning, repeatedly picking herself
up, she had been glad Quen was not there to see
her.


Turning sharply from the tracks at the head
of the valley she could look away down the un-
broken length of the lower canyon. sentineled
by ranks of evergreens with branches weighted
SHIN to their sides by shining armor of snow.
At the rim of the world only cobalt haze
cupped the valley from the distant sawtooth
of peaks that Quen and she had always meant
to climb. Some day.


Martha sat down on the tail of her skis and
buried her head in her woolen-clad knees. After
a moment there was soft whisper over the
uusted surface and the sidewise whoosh of
skid-stop She knew by the sound it had not
been good piece of skiing, 50 of course the
visitor was not Quen. A hand fell on her shoul-
der and young DR.. Randall Presoott's voice,
friendly and everyday, asked, "Is it Quen's
wedding you're upset about?"


She shook her head


Don't lie to me-" said Randy, amiably.
''We've known each other since we were pups?"


''Please, Randy, 60 away"


'Now, look here, Martha Tobin you've got
to brace up. Haven't you realized it was all over
from the minute Suzanne hit town with her
Swiss skiing and her gold eyes? Ever since she
bought herself ski lodge and began inviting
Quen and party up there? Emphasis on Quen."


Too tired to keep up appearances Martha
said, Before Suzanne it was Astrid and before
that, Paula, but Quen always came back"


Suzanne is - Suzanne"


For the first time, Martha head lifted She
looked at loose-jointed Randy, his homely,
wind burned face bent anxiously above her.
"Randy!'


'Well?" His grin was just too late to hide the
pain that had tightened his angular jaw. He
was 50 terribly, deeply different from Quen's
studied dark perfection that she had never
managed really to look at the grown-up Randy
in all the years that they had been in the same
crowd. She had forgotten that he, like Quen,
had become man.


"Randv. what YOU said about Suzanne - is

Over the ridge of their little valley the other
skiers appeared. trailing delicate lengths of
azure shadow. Martha drew quick, painful
breath as she saw Suzanne, tall, her hair gold
halo in the sunset light, and Quen half-a-head
taller gliding beside her protectively, exquisitely
poised as sea gull in fight. Then Quen swung
his skis ever so slightly and came straight to-
ward Martha.


Quen had little jump he wanted to show
her. lust your size, Martha. Thought of you
when tried it last trip up here


She found herself riding beside him, skis
parallel with his. She knew vaguely that Randy
and the others were somewhere behind them;
knew that she and Quen we're not skiing the
slopes of heaven; but those shadowy facts could
not dim the shining certainty that she was again
side by side with Quen, his hand holding hers.
his voice in her ears.


They shot into space together and Marthas
heart, outleaping her skis. very nearly upset
her. Touching snow she fought for balance and
wound up, face flaming with humiliation, in
snowdrift.


Hi, didn't teach you better than that?"
demanded Quen. His dark eyes. wide set in the
smooth gold of his face. laughed down into hers
until an ache in her breast expanded into sitting
physical pain. He reached hand to help her up
and she shut her eyes for moment, loving the
feel of his hard, firm hand under her arm.


Then with shouting of tumpets in her
heart she felt his arm tighten around her and
against her cheek was pressed, as it had been
pressed so many times; the roughness of his
Glacier Park ski coat smelling of honey-sweet
pipe tobacco and clean snow tipped wind


MARTHA" he said. Little Martha" She
fought to steady her breath He was speaking
slowly, almost uncertainty. Life does such
queer things, Martha had to talk with you.

KANSAS CITY, Oct. 5.-The casual
observer, stepping into a Big Six grid
camp this week, would believe himself
in a war zone


On every hand is the frightened,
whispered talk of anticipated air raids.
On the field coaches feverishly drill
their squads in all known defense
moves against aerial bombardments.

point the Jayhawks hope to wipe out

PARIS, July 5.-New diplomatic

because that island commands the

is near the sea lanes between Britain,s
Far Eastern outposts, Hong Kong and
Singapore.


The British government disclosed
on June p that Britain and France
had told Japan to keep of Hainan

with possible complications

IHE DRUMMER BOY shown on Mr.. Stops
cover swearing one ofthefirst official uniforms
that George Washington ordered for his army.
The coat is blue, faced with buff, with buff
waistcoat to match. The trousers and CATERS
are white buckskin - and the hat is black,
bound with gold braid.


This uniform was designed for the New York
and New Jersey troops in 1779- and Wash
ington hoped that it could be made standard
for the entire army, varying only the color of
the facing for troops from different sections.


During the first years of the Revolution,
there was no official uniform. The various
militia companies had their own distinctive
costumes. Certain units of the Massachusetts,
and Connecticut militia even wore red coats,
and were reluctant to give them up despite
the confusion with the British uniform.


Washington recognized the practical diff
iculty of clothing these miscellaneous units of
militia, and recommended buckskin, which
was fairly plentiful. And in l777 the Continen-
tai Congress authorized brown coats for all
Colonial troops, since brown dye was used by
most weavers of home spun. But neither of
these uniforms achieved very wide use.


This lack of uniformity is easy to under
stand when we remember that early in the
war the American troops were really civilians
in revolt. They were embattled farmers, and
all too often they looked like just that.

Greenkeepers at the dozen country
clubs and the public golf courses
around Washington are keeping their
fingers crossed these days. hoping that
1888 will be an unusual year for brown
patch, the deadly fungus that gives
them . big headache and causes golf
ers to moan about the loss of their
putting green's. With the memory
Of the bad year Of 1887 behind them,
the greenkeepers can take plenty of
the cool weather we've been having
lately.


Cool nights without excessive hui
midity keep putting greens in fine
shape, but those hot, damp nights,
without breath Of air stirring, are
the jinxes Of putting greens.


We've been able to get along al
right this year." said o. B. Fits Of
Columbia. But we're keeping our
fingers crossed. We really have had
. good year for putting green's"


Only = Few Spots Now.


Here and there you'll find small
patches Of the dollar" brown patch,
but nowhere will you come across the
big brown spots of moth-eaten grass
that is the sign Of the grass disease
Of other years. Altogether the green
keepers are singing hosannas of Joy
for the cool weather. And can take
q lot more of it.


Golf property around Washington
must be valued at millions OF dollars.
When the putting green's go sour. as
they did last year, that property
takes a nosedive. It's still golf prop
erty. but it isn't such hot stuff. But
your fairways and putting green's
have been plenty good this year, and
they'll stay that way until a spell
Of warm, humid nights comes along.
And then watch out. Your putting
green's can leave overnight.


Science has found some ways to
cut down on the prevalence Of brown
patch. but it hasn't yet found a
positive cure The scientists of the
United States Golf Associations
green's section have found ways to
partially prevent brown patch, but
they haven't yet found any method
to completely eradicate 1t. And the
preventives are expensive.

Climaxing this years Cherry

works frightened the skies above
the Tidal Basin last night, while
1000 spectators crowded its

Last nights audience, gasping
with excitement and amazement
as the "bombs" burst above the
trees, saw the official end Of the
blossom festival. Park officials
however, predicted the blossoms
display will continue for the re-
mainder of the week.

In last nights celebration more
than LOO bombs" and rockets
were used with 500 "bombs" ex-
ploding in the grand finale alone.
High point of the display was the
flaming cherry tree, 40 feet high.


While the festival is officially
over, park officials anticipate con-
tinued crowds of visitors, though
it is not expected that the bios
SONS will be in as good condition
this weekend as they were Sun
day, when $4,000 people treked
