PARIS, May 23.-Informed quarters
ported today that France and Brit
ain had joined in warning Germany
that Czechoslovakia could not be made
the theater of war like that in
Spain.


Both French and Czechoslovak
quarters said the Praha government
had evidence that Sudeten German
Nazis were storing up arms. These
quarters were alarmed by persistent
reports that the war supplies were
coming from Germany.


Informed persons said the British
French warning was delivered by Sir
Neville Henderson, British Ambassa-
dor to Berlin. in one of his visits to
the Wilhelmstrasse during the cur
rent German -Czechoslovak crisis.


France had left no doubt that she
would fight any unprovoked aggression
against Czechoslovakia.


Relief Seen Temporary.


Although the first of three con-
secutive Sunday elections OF COM
munal officials in Czechosiovakia had
passed without a major incident,
French officials viewed the situation
as only temporarily relieved They
insisted the crisis was far from ended.


If German arms were used to start
revolt Of the Sudeten Germans, the
French said, there would be million
incidents" which might afford an ex-
cuse for Adolf Hitler to march into
Czechoslovakia. That, the French
said, would mean war.


Informed quarters said that France
through diplomatic quarters had
warned Berlin there could be no in
tervention in Czechoslovakia like the
intervention-of Germany and Italy
in Spain. They said Frances repre-
sentations were backed by Britain's.


Stefan Osusky, Czecnoslovak Min
lister to Paris, reassured Premier
Edouard Daladier that the Praha gov
ernment was capable Of crushing any
revolt inside the republic and would
seek French aid only if and when
German troops crossed the frontier.


The French cabinet weighed the
crisis and at the same time drafted a
program to put Frances industries
into high gear.


A brief communique after the 2l2-
hour meeting said simply that DEGREES
to stimulate domestic production would
be signed at another session tomorrow
and that the ministers had "delib-
Grated gravely" on the Central Euro
pean situation.


The calmness Of Sundays municipal
elections in Czechoslovokia and the
firm stand taken by France and
Britain against possible German in
reference were considered in Paris
to have eased the tension slightly.


Reports of hurriedly called Nazi
council of Hitler. his diplomatic and
military advisors with the Czech Nazi
leader, Konrad Henlein, led to the
belief, however, that danger was not
yet over.


Fear Hitler May Risk War.


Fears here were based on the pos
sibility Hitler might decide to risk
everything on the chance of quick
war, rather than see what the Fench
consider his plans for domination Of
Central Europe blocked by Czecho-
slovakias refusal to become another
Austria.


In that case, the French spokesman
explained, France was determined to
fight. inevitably drawing Britain into
the conflict with her.


Even French isolationists, who until
the Czech situation became extremely
grave on Saturday had insisted France
had no interest in Czechoslovakia's
fate, agreed France would be bound
to aid her Central European ally in
case of attack.

Evidence of continued improvement
piled up on the Nations trade and in
dustrial ledger this week.


Vitality was most pronounced in the
industrial field where steel production
and carloadings rose to new highs for
the year.


Retail trade improved, but gains
were spotty owing to unusually warm
weather in some regions. Although
nearly all important cities scored gains
over the previous week, most totals
suffered by comparison with last year.


A week ago, various experts said the
fall performance of general business
would depend in large measure on the
automobile industry And this week
for the first time since early May

SO, ,000-a-week level. Wards automo-
tive reports said that orders at fac
tories are at excellent levels"


1000 Workers Recalled.


Two divisions of General Motors
Corp called more than 1000 employees
back to work.


The motor manufacturers, looking
for an increased public buying power,
were cheered by reports of increasing
employment and wages in other in
dustries and estimates which pointed
to generally favorable outlook for
crops.


Not the least important thing which
happened to the automotive industry
was the cutting of prices on steel
sheets. Experts said lower prices for

bile producers.


What the lower quotations would

slight drop in orders for machine

Twice convicted Of flrst-degree
murder for the Staying of his wife,
Will Kinard, colored, is scheduled
to be executed on December 16. The
United States Court of Appeals
which had reversed an earlier con-
viction, today affirmed the trial
courts finding.


The Government charged Kinard
with shooting and killing his wife.
Laura Kinard, on November 6, 1896.
Their children, the only eyewitness,
testified for the Government. The
homicide occurred at 2l7 Third
street SW and the two children,
William kinard, jr.. II, and Pauline
Kinard, 8, took the witness stand
and gave evidence that will send
their father to the chair.


Todays decision of the United
States Court of Appeals held that
Kinard had a fair and impartial
trial and waved aside the defense
contention that the court had er-
roneously charged the jury regard
ing statements made by the defend
ant himself.


Court Upholds Charge.


Associate Justice Justin Miller,
who wrote today's opinion, recalled
that Kinard had twice been convict
ed and that judgment of murder IN
the first degree was reversed by that
tribunal earlier. The ground of re-
versal was that the trial judge had
failed properly to instruct the jury
concerning manslaughter.


The Court OF Appeals said in its
opinion today that no objection or
exception was taken to the charge
as given by the trial judge when the
question YVES raised for the first time
on appeal.


Kinard, through his counsel, con-
tended the trial courts charge was
erroneous because he had improperly
emphasized evidence unfavorable to
the accused. The appellate tribunal
today, however, held that the court
had instructed the jury properly and
gave accurate instruction concern
ing self defense, which had con-
tended that the mother had knife
in her hand shortly before the shoot
ing and that she was about to throw
a salt-shaker at the father. The
Government had produced evidence
showing that the woman had been
shot six times, once in the left arm
and five times in the chest and alb
domen, and six empty cartridges
were taken from the appellants gun
and were put into evidence.


Stay Follows Appeal.


Kinard's date OF execution was
set for last July 8, but due to the
fact that his case was on appeal,
Justice Jesse C. Adkins granted
stay of execution until December is.


Arguing the case for the Govern
ment were United States Attorney
David A. Pine and Assistant United
States Attorney John w. Fihelly,
as we'll as Roger Robb, who was an
assistant United States attorney at
the time of the trial and is now
engaged in the private practice of
law.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 22.-Fighting
came ominously close to Shanghai

The battle, which began before dawn

largest in the Shanghai area since
the japanese captured the city last
November.


Scores of foreign residents of the
Hungjao area were endangered. many
rushing to the International Settle
ment for safety.


The guerrillas, believed to number
about 500, apparently were we'll armed
with machine guns and rifles and were
maintaining constant fire.


Dozens of Japanese trucks loaded
with reinforcements raced westward
through the outer portion of the In
ternational Settlement to take up the
battle after the regular outposts re-
ported they were unable to cope with
the attack.


Shortly after the battle started the
japanese closed the Hungjao area to
civilian entry or exit, trapping for
eigners who had remained in their
homes. and preventing others, who
were in the city, from returning home.


There were not many foreigners in
the western section Of Hungjao, but
those in that section reported by tele-
phone that fighting was going on
nearby and that machine-gun bullets
were sweeping the area constantly.
. Numerous japanese aircraft were
accommodating the district, but had
not entered the conflict.


International Settlement police re-
ported sniping between japanese and
Chinese troops had broken out near
the western borders of the Settlement,
indicating the Chinese had penetrated
deep into the japanese lines.

reports said irregulars had defeated

West opened a diamond. Dummys
ace won the trick, and the king of
spades was then played. Puzzling as to
how to get into his hand to draw
trumps, declarer returned a diamond.
East won and led a third round.
When South trumped with the ten
West overtrumped with the Jack
and returned club. East captured
dummy's king with his ace and led a
fourth diamond. This time declarer
trumped with the ace of spades, and
West discarded a heart. Declarer
now played hearts, but West trumped
the third round, and East's queen of
clubs took the setting trick,


Declarer would actually have made
his contract if he had overtaken the
king of spades with his ace, followed
with the queen and then played hearts.
However, the almost certain way to
insure the contract is far simpler.
When East got in with the second
diamond and played the third round
declarer should have thrown a club.
East would have played fourth dia-
mond, whereupon declarer should
discard his remaining club. Declarer
would then trump East's last dia-
mond, and West would overtrump.
Then at last declarer would have been
able to run club and enter his hand
to draw trumps.


Hands of this type occur frequent
ly and are just as frequently mis-
played. The principle is this: When
in danger of being repeatedly over
ruf1ed discard all your losers be-
fore trumping. Then when you finally
trump you will be overtrumped once
but will subsequently be able to draw
the remaining trumps.

PUEBLO, Colo, April 9 Q.N.S0 .
Rescue crews were dispatched to-
day from eastern Colorado points
to dig out two Missouri Pacific
trains, lost and unheard from for
the past "a hours, but which were
located a few miles east of Horace,
Kan, late last night, according to
Ralph E. Allen, Colorado division
trainmaster.


Allen said roundabout communi-
cations, made necessary when
Snowstorms, which swept the ma
ton the past few days, tore down
all telegraph lines, gave informa-
ton leading to finding the trains
but did not divulge the condition
of the passengers or crew.


Allen said one train, due at
Pueblo at 10:45 a. m. yesterday,
was located near Marquette, Kan,
and the other, bound for Kansas
City, was last heard from near
Scott City. Kan. There were 80
or 40 passengers on the eastbound
train, Allen declared.


Snowplows and helper engines
have been sent to evacuate the
stalled trains.

- ABY animals and human babies are
IL pretty much alike in one thing. They
both want affection and companion
- ship, and if they don't get it they react
in the same way - they cry.


Not all baby animals can make crying
sounds, of course, and to that extent the
analogy falls down. But baby baboon can
screech and scream and cry louder and longer
than any human baby. 1t was such lusty
and insistent youngster that arrived at the
animal hospital in the New York Geological
Park recently. She was only few months
old.


The first halliday in the isolation of the
quarantine room at the hospital she yelled
until the veterinarian realized he had to do
something, as much for his own peace of mind
as the baby's. So he telephoned to the parks
nursery, and half an hour later truck deliv-
cred big white rabbit and bundle of lettuce
leaves.


Leaves and rabbit went into the baboon's
cage Nothing ever surprises or startles rab-
bit. It was interested only in that bundle of
lettuce leaves.


The advent of companion hushed the
baby baboon instantly. however. She was
frightened at first, but as courage returned
she made few tentative rushes toward the
rabbit. 1t neither jumped nor bit; obviously
it was friend Within an hour she was hug
ging the rabbit, searching its fur for "feas,"
straddling its back and tugging at its long
ears. When the play became too rough the
rabbit simply hoped and sent the baboon
tumbling. That was the only kind of resent
ment it ever showed And from that day the
little baboon was lively, oontented speci-
men.

Don't look now. folks, but can that
be the rejuvenated Cleveland Indians
and Bill Terry's terrific Giants who
have just dropped the first series OF
their respective Eastern and Western
invasions?


Only week ago, they were saying
that Oscar Witt had put some T. N. T.
into the Tribes breakfast food this
year, and that from now on they
wouldn't be like Little Bo Peeps lost
sheep when they made their tours
round the circuit. And they were
saying. too, that Terry's Terriers had
uncovered a batting punch no one
suspected they had-a wallop that
almost made them look like feared
American Leaguers.


But all that was before both out
fits left home and the friendly feel
of their own parks. And now the
little brides are starting to whisper
that it's probably the same old set
OF Indians. after all. and that Terry's
Terriers looked like real sluggers
against the Eastern stooges, like the
Brooklyns and the Phillies, but now
that they've met up with the tougher
Western foes they're finding some-
thing else than pushover opposition.


Expected to Be Different.


For years Cleveland's been famous
as the team that looked like champs
at home and tramps everywhere else
in the circuit This spring, however,
Witt concentrated on building up a
new spirit, but from the looks of the
first series in Washington, it either
hasn't taken yet, or it's going to miss
completely. The Senators squeaked
through with 10 decision in l3 IN
nings Wednesday and yesterday hung
an 8-6 beating on the Witt warriors,
largely through Johnny Stones homer
with the bases loaded.


In the Giants early campaigning
the Polo Grounds cheering and chow
der society had been taking the Bronx
apart telling of the wonders Terry's
boys were doing with the big bat. But
that was while the Phils and Dodgers
pitchers were serving them up to the
Giants. mostly in that neat little affair,
the Polo Grounds, and its inviting
sight and left field stands.


For the last three days, the Giants
have been performing in the vast
reaches of Cincinnati's Crosley Field.
and things have been so different
they've dropped two Of three games.
Yesterday Harry Gumbert went to the
wars and was whipped, So. by the
rude Reds. largely through the help
Of an obliging two-run error by Master
Mel OFT.

his chief rivals, the Chicago Cubs,
opened up wide on the throttle and
knocked the ears completely off the
futile Phillies, 21-2, with an 18-hit
attack that featured a l2-run splurge
in the eighth inning. And a rookie,
Paul Epperly, held the Phils to six hits
In his first major league start.

first place in the American League by

"Most Harmless Liars"


OUR OLD MAN thought that hunting and fish
" ing liars were the most harmless of all liars,
and that liars about amatory adventures were
the least interesting. He liked fighting liars
that is fellows who lied about fights they had
in their time.


Our old man was struck by one similarity in
nearly all fighting lies. He said he had found
that almost invariably the fighting liar had his
fights with great big guys. Our old man said
that in years of listening to fight lies he had
never heard but one man say that the fellow
he fought was a little bit Of a chap, and even
then he added that the little chap had two guns
and knife.


Our old man said it was curious thing about
mean liars, that they could always find large
and attentive audience, especially if their lies
were damaging to some fellow man.

Failing to swing a deal with the

A real incubator for high school

Each branch Is a hotbed Of COM

ceive their early training and

sports, and when they reach high

Galapagos Archipelago, July 81
Charles Island. the one-time refuge of
Baroness Eloise Wehrborn and her
court" was the anchorage of the
cruiser Houston and its presidential
party today.


1t was the first inhabited island of
the Galapagos group which the Hous-
ton visited since arriving among the
islands Sunday. President Roose-
velt did not 60 ashore. but members
of his party left the ship to explore
the island and take gifts from the
President to the Wittmer family

his wife, Margaret, and their three
children.


Locale Of Strange Mystery.


The island was the locale of one Of
the strangest mystery death stories
ever to come out of the tropics The
story involved supposed paradise
once ruled by the German baroness.


In 1884 the bodies of two men who
had died of thirst were found on
bleak Marchena Island, one of the
Galapagos group. They were identi-
fled as Arthur Rudolph Lorenz. former
Partisan, and Norwegian sailor
named Nuggerood.


How the men reached Marchena
Island was never determined There
was no trace Of any boat having taken
them there


Later it was learned the baroness
and companion. Robert PhilipsoA,
who possibly could have shed some
light on the mystery, sailed from the
South Seas, never to be heard from
again.

shortly before noon, headed for Gard
ner Bay in Hood Island, run of
about four hours, where it was to
anchor overnight.

text:
Washingtonians and residents
of the Eastern Seaboard witnessed
an old-fashioned sort of "black-
out" yesterday evening when the
moon was in total eclipse.


Partially obscured by the earth's
shadow, the moon rose at 4:45
p. m. and could not again be seen
by the naked eye until 6:07, when
thin, copper-colored slice became
visible.


LIKE OLD COPPER


From then until 7:15, when the
full moon was again shining IN the
star.lighted heavens, the celestial
satellite was the color Of old cop
per, easily seen except when scud-
ding clouds sped across the skies.


Naval and Georgetown observa-
tory officials said that the eclipse
was one of the brightest they had
seen. The brightness, they said,
was caused by the suns light
reaching it through the outer at.
mosphere Of the earth.


The course of last nights eclipse
was plotted three years ago and
followed the schedule as mlnutely
as though earthly scientists had
control Of the phenomenon from
the beginning.


Astronomer John E. Willis, of
the Naval Observatory, and Father
Paul A. McNally, director of the
Georgetown Observatory, closely
watched the lunar act through
powerful telescopes and photo
graphed the process from begin
ming to end.


PHENOMENON EXPLAINED


While the eclipse was caused by
the shadow of the earth passing
between the sun and the moon,
both sun and moon appeared to
be in the sky five minutes after
the moon rose. This, the scien.
fists said, was caused by refrac-
ton, bent light rays making both
sun and moon seem higher than
they actually were.


Although plenty of advance no
tice had been given of the sched-
uled eclipse, operators at both
observatories received many tele-
phone calls from persons wanting
to know what it was all about.

Sweden from a fashion view
point. The colorful dress of the
Russian, the Swiss and the Mexi.

lar and full sleeves gathered at
the wrist. Accessories are ex-
tremely gay, jewelry is heavy,
and millinery varies from tall,
pointed caps to knotted scarfs.


My personal favorite Of the
Swedish adaptations is Gale
Pages full-skirted, sleeveless coat
dress, which has fitted bodice
laced up the front. It is linen,
taking its shade of blue from
the Swedish flag, and is coupled
with a yellow handkerchief linen
blouse which also takes its color
from the Swedish national ban
ner. The blouse has high,
turnover collar, but the sleeves
are only elbow length.

uANANOQUE. Canada. Aug. 13.-
Wheh President Roosevelt and Ca
madam Premier Mackenzie King dedi-
cate the new international bridge
across the st. Lawrence River at the
Thousand Islands on August 18, they
viii add another stone to one of the

the American-Canadian border.


The writer has just travelled along
hundreds of miles of this border while
studying the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence
deep waterway project which long has
been under consideration by the two
countries.


After IL years spent in Europe, 1t
was an almost unbelievable expert
ence. Gone were passport formalities,
customs formalities, currency formali-
ties, the usual half-hour wait beneath
the prying eyes and fingers of guards
and officials.


The writer had and declared a
portable typewriter. a candid camera
and pair of field glasses-all OBJ
jects of suspicion in Europe. There
was no trouble.


Travelled Along Border.


In Canada he Travelled along the
border-something that had best not
be done In Europe these days. But
here there was nothing but courtesy.
The language was the same. the peo-
pie seem the same, signs were differ
ent-being in both French and Eng
lish-automobiles were the same
money the same (since American and
Canadian currency had equal accept
ance, the exchange being practically
at par.


The writer paid for something with
a IS Canadian banknote and got In
change two American dollars, two
Canadian dollars and mixed silver
Of both countries.


Frequently you see boundary mark
ers defining the 5.526 miles of border
between the United States Gnclud-
ing Alaska) and Canada. There are
8,060 such monuments.


On one side of the monument you
Gee the words United States" and
international Line and on the other
Canada" and international Line" "

the date Of the treaty governing that
section Of the border.


Swaths Cut Through Forests.


Occasionally you come across a
border forest strip where a swath 20
feet wide has been cut through the
woods to keep the boundary line open
and the border monuments visible.
Fifteen hundred miles of forest area
have been so cleared.


At international highways hand
some ornamental concrete shafts
designate the boundary, one on each
side of the road Bridges are marked
with bronze tablets. When the baum
dairy runs through q body Of water
the monuments are placed on the
shore.


The work of the American and
Canadian commissioners Of the In
ternational Boundaries Commission,
Thomas Riggs and Noel Ogilvie. has
met with high praise. Typical of the
feeling across the border Is the fact
that the two commissioners have been
warm friends from tho time IS years
ago when they were young surveyors
together in the Cascade Mountains.


The writer had occasion to cross
back into the United States twice to
visit strategic points of the Great
Lakes-St. Lawrence project. On
neither occasion was his name asked
Only the fact that he was born In
Ohio, his wife In Tennessee and his
daughter In Rome. Italy. Even this
last birthplace caused no comment.
The border seemed more symbolic
than real.

Associated Press Financial Writer


The Nations busines found encour-
agement this week in the automobile
industry.


Although actual motor production
dropped to new low for the year.
word came from leading automotive
centers that the industry was prepar-
ing to swing into a new productior
season.


Detroit provided an example of
what heavier production will mean to
industry and business at large Max
ers prepared for the output of new
models. thousands Of workers were
called back to work Within two days
1850 families had withdrawn from
welfare rolls.


Meanwhile the Department Of Com
merce reported employment increases
in other centers-although it indi-
Gated the increases were modest


Statistics which crossed the desk
Of business analysts during the week
showed the effects of the midsummer
season.


Electricity Production Up.


Carloadings, steel and motor output
slackened. Electricity production
made a contra seasonal rise aided in
part by increased demand for power
in the Detroit industrial area.


Soaring heat caused retail trade
to wilt in some sections Neverthe-
less. the Commerce Department re-
ported:


THE forces Of recovery throughout
the country moved forward steadily,
though slowly"


Experts attached considerable i'm
portance to the fact that. while dollar
turnover Of goods showed losses. actual
sales of goods probably equaled or
even excelled last years totals owing
to lower price levels


Wholesale Trade Advances.


Wholesale trade moved quietly
ahead. although reports from leading
centers said heat had kept many buy
ers out of the market


In the industrial sector scrap steel
prices rose. Experts noted that the
steel industry leaned mainly on motor
makers and miscellaneous manufac-
turers for support.


Meanwhile the construction indus
try, aided by an increased number of
Federal projects, afforded some prom
ise of improvement.


Iron Age said that an increased
number of private construction jobs
was on hand. but explained that this
indicated buying Of steel only in the
smaller tonnage brackets. Still absent
among steel buyers was the railroad
industry Until the railroads come
into the market, steel output will lack
important support


The American Iron and Steel Insti-
tute reported steel production at 39.4
per cent of capacity. In the previous
week it was 1913, 323 per cent a month
ago and 846 per cent in the like 1887
week.


Motor production as reported by
Wards dropped to 1890 units from
l4,77l the preceding week and 103.250
in the corresponding period year ago.
Corloadings Lower.


The Association of American Rail-
roads reported carloadings at 584,05o
in the week ended August 6, slight
downturn from the previous week and
238 per cent under the figure for the
like week last year. The Edison Elec-
trio Institute said power production
totaled 2.115,847, 900 kilowatt hours in
the week ended August s. This wa
up little from the previous week but
down GA per cent from year ago.


The Commerce Department said that
lin the following cities retail trade
was ahead of last year: Wilmington.
Memphis, New Orleans. Norfolk and
Jacksonville. In Milwaukee. Washing
ton, Atlanta and Omaha the decline
was so small as to be without signifl-
canoe. Chicago retail establishments
continued to show encouraging signs
of improvement, with special sales OF
summer goods enjoying success. Trade
improved also in Boston when fair
weather arrived"

GRAFTON, Ohio, Dec. "a
U.NSO and neighbors
did their best today to restore
some of the luster of Christmas
for Geraldine Rousseau, II, and
her sister. Sarah, 8, innocent VIC
tins of Ohio's Christmas tree
tragedy.


The task of those kind-hearted
persons was not an easy one for
the father of Geraldine and Sarah
lay dead, and the spark of life
flickered uncertainty in their
mother-all because Of Christ
mas tree which was to have made
the holiday little brighter in the
poorly furnished but neat Rous-
Eeau home.


GIFTS, BUT SAD ONES


Geraldine wanted a little sew
ing machine and her sister hoped
Santa would bring her new doll.
They probably will receive those
gifts and many more-citizenS
deeply touched by the tragedy
will see to that-but their father,
william Rousseau, 81, is gone and
it was doubtful whether their
mother, Mrs. Minnie Rousseau, 20,
would survive the day.


The parents were shot down
while cutting a spruce tree on the
farm of white.bearded, 84-year-old
william Case. Having spent their
last few pennies for 5 and TO-
cent toys in Cleveland, the unem-
ployed truck driver and his wife
had no money for a Christmas
tree. Yet they dreaded disap-
pointing their two young daugh.
ters.


SHOOTING ADMITTED


The journey home from Cleve-
land took them past the Case
farm where stood dozens of ever
greens. After cutting the top
from one and starting toward
their antiquated auto, Rousseau
and his wife were fired upon.


Case, in Lorain county Jail at
Elyria, freely admitted the shoot
ing. He was being held there
without charge while the prose
cutor decides whether to file
charges or leave the matter for
grand jury consideration.


With long gray hair and a
flowing beard, the aged widower
could easily take the part Of
Santa Claus had he not been
cast in a different Christmas
role.


TRANSMISSION FOR MOTHER


He said complaints to the
sheriff had failed to stop the
wholesale theft of his trees so he
decided to stand guard with his
shotgun.


They were stealing my trees;
I had to do something" Sheriff
Carl Ffnegan quoted Case as
saying.


The sheriff gave a pint of his
own blood for a TRANSMISSION for
Mrs. Rousseau, but she failed to
rally. There were 80 shotgun pei,
let's in her side, breast and hip
and physicians at Elyria Me
mortal Hospital said her chances
for recovery were slim.


Rousseau had not been regularly
employed for six years.

Three aeronautical agreements be-
tween the United States and Canada
were reached yesterday through an ex-
change of notes between Secretary of

Herbert Marler.

l. Air navigation


2. Reciprocal issuance OF airman
certificates.

tiflcates of airworthiness concerning
airplanes for export.


They comprise the 10th bilateral air
accord reached between the United
States and other nations. The others
are with Belgium, Denmark, Germany,
Great Britain, Ireland, Italy, Norway,
Sweden and Union OF South Africa.


Superseding an accord reached in

Canada, the air navigation agreement
provides for the recognition by each
government. for flights over its ter
ritory, Of certificates or licenses issued

craft and airmen; equality of treat
ment with regard to aircraft facilities;

tain zones, and compliance with local
regulations, including those relating

the Grace liners Santa Paula and
Santa Lucia and the Puerto Rico
liner Coamo.


Visibility at Quarantine was only
250 feet at 8 am. and at Sandy Hook
observers said it was a half mile.

A while back 1t was considered
smart" for girls to paddle around in
the rain without rubbers or raincoat.
There was no tangible reason for this
foolish fashion but because 1t was
fashion many of us went without pro-
lection and suffered from wet feet,
invited nasty head colds, and ruined
our best shoes.


Then somehow fashion changed
Perhaps beauty realized she wasn't
beautiful with her nose red and run
ming, and chills creeping up and down
her spine. So she began to get some
sense.


Before you knew it stylists had de-
signed attractive, gay waterproofs and
footgear. Even the old-fashioned um-
brella turned into something colorful
and transparent. And today's smart
young things deck themselves in this
new rainy day finery. and actually look
askance at the girl who trips through
puddles without rubbers!


Miss Today knows it is smart to keep
healthy and to keep beautiful. Actu-
ally, throughout England and America,
girls and women take great pride in
preserving the appealing, lovely curves
Of youth and guarding their looks from
the ravages of any illness.


Girls realize that little head cold
can develop swiftly into a dangerous
chest condition. especially if one is IA
tigued or slightly under par. So they
take no risks They meet rainy day
as they should, with bodies protected
from dampness, and faces smiling from
the knowledge that a few raindrops
cannot rob them of their beauty!


Even the leading cosmetic firms took
up the rainy day question and gave us
water resistant colors for our cheeks
and lips, and softly adherent powders
which defy moisture. So even if you
do prefer to walk in the rain without
an umbrella you may be assured that
your complexion will retain the art
.istry you applied before Drawing the
storm!


Ask to see these water -repellent cos
metics-rouge, lipstick. powder and eye
cosmetique. AS walking has become
fad, you will want to know about
such cosmetics for that walking date
one rainy afternoon!

NEW YORK, Dec. PA Christ
mas benediction laid over Wall
Street today as trading in stocks
and bonds ended for the week.


The bankers, the brokers, the
clerks and the secretaries poured
out from the tall buildings, then
scuttled underground to their sub
ways, out Of the range Of bitter
winds from an overcast sky.


Ahead of them were two days of
rest before the tickers start chat
tering again next Tuesday.


Behind them. its great branches
whipping in the gales, they left
Wall Streets annual reminder of
the season-a 58-foot spruce tree
blazing with colored lights and
burning white star.


The huge evergreen suddenly be-
came one of the loneliest objects
in the big town. Until today its
topmost branches could look out
upon dozens Of tiny relatives, lighted
In surrounding brokerage offices.

HENDAYE, co-Spanish
Border, July 20 GN.S).-Bitter
street fighting ragged in the Cata-
Ian stronghold Of Gandesa today
as Spanish government troops
forced their way to the center of
the city, slowly driving nationalist
forces before them.


I'm London, the Daily Herald
published a Barcelona dispatch
citing private, unconfirmed ad-
vices that government troops had
captured Gandesa after fierce
fighting.)


Reports received here from the
Spanish governments provisional
capital at Barcelona said the gov
eminent troops were slowly but
surely mopping up the enemy
units, many of which were still
holding out in fortified churches
and public buildings.


PRESS FORWARD
! Other government legions, push
ling steadily forward, occupied vii
.flabla and another village south
of Gandesa.


Within the last 80 hours, it
was claimed, the government
forces have captured more terri
tory than in all their other three
main offensiveS-those of Bru-
nete, Belchite and Teruel.


The charging government
forces, who assaulted Gandesa
after crossing the Ebro River,
drove the nationalists before them
with hand grenades, rifle fire and
bayonets.


Most of Gandesa was reported
in possession of government troops.
Complete occupation was ex-
pected momentarily, according to
Barcelona.


VITAL JUNCTION


The fierce fighting in the impor-
tant city, a vital junction Of
numerous Catalan highways, was
the chief engagement provoked by
the government offensive, designed
to relieve General frances pres
sure against Valencia in the south.


So far the government has re-
captured scores of towns west of
the Ebro and captured between
1000 and 5000 prisoners. BARGE
Iona claimed a net advance of
more than 20 miles along the en-
tire 93-mile Catalan front.

HENDAYE. France Aug. 20.-Span-

cisco Franco opened what apparently
was a carefully planned offensive.


The insurgents attacked in force
on the Ebro River front, south of
Gandesa, where they reported the
first line Of government trenches in
the Pandos Mountains had been occu-
pied and the second line was being
attacked today.


Bulletins from Barcelona said, how
ever, the government lines had held
against the assault and had not lost

Combined Drive Expected.


Observers believed Gen. Franco had
given orders to his field commanders
to wipe out the governments Ebro
salient this week end so a combined
campaign against Barcelona and Va
lencia could start from consolidated
positions.


First indications that a major offen-

insurgent authorities Cancelled passes
for exit to France as they had done
frequently in the past before big
drives.


Insurgent military leaders confirmed
later that Gen. Franco himself would
lead q new offensive. The general
issimo named Gen. Juan Vigon,
former chief Of staff of the northern
insurgent army, as chief of his per-
sonal staff. Several insurgent officers
who had been on leave were recalled
to duty, effective tomorrow.

were under way. italian shock divisions

NEW YORK, Sept. 24.-Tourists re-
turning from Poland this fall are
bringing back As their most precious
souvenirs specimens Of hand-spun and
hand-woven linens made in peasant
cottages.


Recent activities Of society formed
to foster peasant handicraft indus
tries have resulted in bringing into
shops In Wilno, Warsaw, Cracow and
other large Polish cities examples Of
an ancient art where travellers from
abroad could see them. and the result
OF that was that the articles displayed
went like hot cakes.


These Polish linens are different
from anything most Americans ever
saw. For one thing, they are alive with
brilliant colors-rich and vivid hueS
created by dipping the threads tn
homemade dyes In the farmhouses
where the cloth Is made In primitive
looms. Another characteristic of the
native textiles Is that they are 50
tough they are virtually imperishable.
The peasants use them for horse
blankets and for tarpaulins for mar
ket carts. Made into brocades, hang
ings, table linens, towels, scarves,
blouses, bedspreads and every variety
OF garment and cloth furnishing, they
are embellished with embroidery,
drawn-thread work and lace and
frightened with background designs
Of complicated geometrical patterns in
various harmonious but strong colors.
Some OF them are made Of cloth that
has a linen warp and = wool weft of
contrasting shade.


Linen has never been much of q
factory product in Poland. The greater
part OF the cloth is made by women
in farmhouses and village homes, by
patient. painstaking methods evolved
through centuries Of cottage manu-
facture. Nearly every cottage has 4
crude loom. worked indoors in the
cold weather and often set out in the
sun in the summer. The decoration
and embroidering Of linen and the
linen articles takes even longer than
the manufacture Of the cloth.

There are other amenities

Florida resorts that add conSid-

making an annual trip South.

eliminates the shock Of travelling
from the cold North to the warm
South; for the cars are scien-

the train comes under the warm
Florida sun.


Again, the service and cuisine
In the dining cars is justly famous.


And there are special lounge
recreation cars that put the final
touch toward completing the ideal
Of a "home and club on rails"

equipment only, including bed
room-drawing room compartment

urious appointments and includes
the de luxe reclining-seat coaches

Florida, both completely air-condi-
toned, leave Washington daily
for east-coast and west-coaSt win.

mestic copper price was held at 10

inquiry.

Amid thousands of visitors, but

doah XIV was crowned this after
noon by Admiral Richard E.
Byrd.


Viewing the coronation of AIDE
Iaide Moffett was Miss Gladys
Harris, queen In her own right,

Apple Blossom Festival in Kent.

IDEAL WEATHER


Sunny skies and typical sum-
mer weather greeted the thousands
Of visitors descending on this his
torical town for it's fifteenth an.
iaual tribute to its greatest indus
try. Visitors arrived by plane,
bus and special trains and
excursions being operated by two
railroads. Thousands poured into
the city via private automobiles.


Forecasts given festival officials
by the Weather Bureau in Wash
ington have assured a fair-weather
festival. Rain, which often has
marred the gala event in the past,

ing. The vendors were the first to

city last night.

firemen's torchlight parade here

sponsored by the Charlie Rouss
Fire Company. of which Admiral
Byrd, Harry K. Thaw and United

members.

to direct the traffic expected here
today and tomorrow.

standing visitors was the Bricken-
bridge Band and Drum Corps,
whose fire company will lead the
firemen's parade tonight.


Thirty princeSSes arriving here
yesterday were guests of the fes-
tival committee this morning and
were taken on a tour of historic
Winchester.

program were the presentation
Of the historical pageant, In
6pringtin1e," at the Handley High
School bowl, and the coronation
Of Queen Shenandoah XIV.

various orchards by the Queen and
her court; an exhibition of stunt
flying and parachute jumping;
the Queens luncheon; numerous
band concerts; a vocal concert by
the V.M.I. Glee Club, of Lexing-
ton; street dances, and the days
finale of the official apple blossom
dance at the Sarah Zane Fire Hall.

The War Department has struck
its colors and sounded retreat in a
battle with diplomats for office
space in the old State, War and
Navy Building.


Built for all three departments,
the historic structure across from
the White House executive Offices, at
Pennsylvania avenue and Seven
teenth streets NV, now is big
enough only for the State Depart
ment.


Secretary Of War Woodring an
nounced yesterday that the Army
would abandon the field and transfer
all its activities now housed In the
old building alongside the diplomats
to the Munitions Building, at Con-
stitution avenue and Nineteenth
street NV, about January /.


The transfer will encourage closer
cooperation between the Army and
Navy, since the latter already is
housed in the Munitions Building


1t is temporary measure. how
ever. The Navy is cramped in the
Munitions Building, erected in war
time as temporary structure. Con-
gress has authorized funds to con-
struct new War Department Build
ing, but several years will be re-
quired for its completion. Ground
has not been broken for 1t yet.


The temporary transfer will cul-
inmate a move begun during the
World War, which has resulted In
War Department activities being
scattered through 10 different build
ings here.


Sudden expansion of State, War
and Navy Department activities dur
ing the World War made the old
three-department building made
quate for their needs and the diplo-
mats began taking over more and
more space. Completed in 1888 after
II years of construction work, 1t then
was reputed to be the finest and
largest office building in the world,
but now is dwarfed by many of the
departmental buildings constructed
since the World War.

gripping this section.

not occupied at the time The care
taker noticed the flames and called
county f1remen who poured water into
the three-story building for more than
five hours.

The yacht, a small cruiser, the
Memory. was reported late yester-
day in distress near Point No
Point, her rudder carried away.
The Calypso searched the bay
and the river near the point with
out success, and finally reported
to Coast Guard headquarters that
it was believed the yacht had been
towed away by some passing craft.


ASK FOR HELP


Identity Of the disabled yacht
was not Immediately learned, as
there are six boats of that name
on the bay.


Word of the plight of the yacht
was first received from the
freighter Steel Scientist, which
was outward bound down the bay
when she observed the yacht fly
ing a distress signal.


The freighter heaved to, and
men on board the yacht asked
that the Coast Guard be notified
that the craft had lost its rudder
and needed help.


This message was radioed by
the freighter to Coast Guard head
quarters at Norfolk. and the
Calypso, which was at Baltimore,
was directed to proceed at once to
assist the yacht.


SEARCH IN VAIN


The Calypso left Baltimore at
1920 last night, and arriving at
the location given by the freighter,
searched for hours without sue
cess.


The Weather Bureau reported
there was a high wind on the bay
last night, and for a time it was
feared the small yacht might have
dragged its anchor and either
been driven ashore or sunk, but no
wreckage was sighted, and Coast
Guard officials believe the craft
is safe.

The plight OF the Kern children
Betty, 8, Phillis, 8; Barbara, S, and

They found Betty mothering the

But by last night Betty's charges

Then Mrs. Thomas arrived. helped
Betty dress the younger children and

The blond, handsome children still

the police that something untoward

1t was anything too serious.


"1nky," the black cat, was not for

The two guardian policemen were

cry County probation authorities at

/ Meanwhile, seeing that the children

Twas the night after Christmas, the children abed-
The living room looked like junk-deale shed;
The train was agog-gog half off of the track
doll baby, armless, lay fiat on its back;
An elephant sat with hole in his side
And the drum had slit in its head, long and wide
The cavalry troop, horses, riders and all,
Were pitched on their faces-a terrible fall.
The dump truck was dumped with its load the floor
And the headlights burned out to be lit never more.
The whiskers were pulled from the cat and the dog
Was bespattered with candy-and was the frog;
The airplane had crashed with its to the wall,
And the bugle quite dented, was past all recall;
The bus and the tractor the donkeys hee-haw,
Had all been demolished by hammer and saw.
The Christmas tree stood in the corner, like stone
And lighted the wreckage, forlorn and alone;
Poor mother, with poultices placed on her head
Fell asleep on chair before going to bed,
And father, for playing from morning till night
Was paying the penalty serving him right.
The house was in havoc, the servants were gone
With no one to clear up the debris till morn;
And this Is the picture as I understand,
OF the night after Christmas all over the land

NORTH CHICAGO, Ill, July l9.-
Police and deputy sheriffs fired a tear
gas attack today on pickets blocking
entrance to the strike-bound Chicago
Hardware Foundry Co. plant. A half
dozen women pickets were knocked
to the ground.


Pickets fought the officers in hand
to-hand encounters while tear gas
bombs and shells burst all around.
About so regular and special deputies
and city police from North Chicago
and nearby towns launched the at
tack after giving the pickets five
minutes to "break it up"


Officers carried guns. but did not
use them. They fired tear gas from
pistols and threw gas bombs. About
so gas missiles burst within a few
minutes.


Pickets Reform Lines.


After the first clash. the pickets
retreated, formed their ranks again
and gave way anew as the deputies
advanced, hurting tear gas bombs into
the crowd


At length, the demonstrators were
driven to point three blocks from the
plant. They scattered into nearby
fields and made no further attempt
to return to the foundry for the time
being


During the battle, the pickets threw
stones, bottles and empty tear gas
cartridges at the officers.


The policemen moved back to the
plant after the engagement.


Standing in front of it, wiping tear
streaming eyes. was lone woman,
holding aloft the American flag.


Ordered to Disperse.


Chief of Police j. j. Novak Of
North Chicago went down the line
of pickets massed east and west across
Commonwealth avenue at the main
gate of the plant which has been
strikebound for six weeks.


The chief told the pickets to dis
perse within five minutes or the
officers would force them to scatter


The pickets remained at their posts
When the time limit expired, the
officers moved in.


In an instant individual fights be-
tween officers and pickets broke out
Officers welded clubs and black kjacks
while loosing the tear gas attack.


Dozens Of pickets, watching the
officers gathering, had obtained pals

lection from the gas.

in the first few seconds five or six
women pickets were knocked down.

Street demonstrations took place

NEW HUNGARIAN NOTE.

By the Associated Press.


CANTON, Oct PA gigantic con-
tlagration threatened to destroy this
South China metropolis today as fires
roared into residential districts after
burning out the business sections


Japanese dynamite squads blasted
firebreaks around the burning areas
in an attempt to halt the spreading
flames, while foreign volunteers aided
in trying to save foreign buildings.


Dynamite was the only weapon the
f1re-fghters could use, since the blast
ing of Canton's reservoirs before the
Chinese fled had completely disrupted
water supplies.


Some small fires broke out in the
International Settlement on Shameen
Island, but were quickly extinguished
and shift of the wind carried the
flames away from the island after a
mile of waterfront buildings across
the 80-foot creek had been destroyed.


Munitions Explode.


Many buildings on the island were
damaged yesterday by three terrific
explosions of munitions which the
Chinese had abandoned in Wongsha
Railway Station. The blasts scattered
fragments over the entire settlement,
breaking windows and blowing out
shutters.


The United States Consulate-Gen-
eral suffered slight damage, plaster
falling from ceilings due to the con-
cussion when the munitions dumps
went up. There were no casualties
and harm to the building was trivial.
The Dutch Consulate was similarly
shaken.


The Associated Press photographer
near the station at the time was hit
in the back by falling stones.


The Saichuen and Honam districts
of the city were the worst damaged.

ment. Anna called her book BLACK

was confined to her bed. Often she
was too weak to write; at these times
her mother took dictation from the
bedside.


Finally, in 1877, Black Beauty"
was published, but Anna Sewell did
not live to see the tremendous sales
it attained. She had sold her book
to her publishers outright for q few
pounds-less than 500. Anna died
within year, but her book lived ou-
her single literary work.

MANILA, Philippine Islands,
Aug. / GNSD. D.-Pinning their
fading hopes upon the fact no
wreckage was found at an oil spot
discovered on the Pacific, Army
and Navy craft today doggedly
continued their search of the
Philippine coastline for the Hawaii
Clipper which vanished Friday
with Is persons aboard.


Although most aviation experts
believed the huge oil slick found
525 miles southeast of Manila, at
almost exactly the point where
the clipper last radioed its posi-
ton, marked the ocean grave of
the big silver flying boat and its
occupants, Pan American Airways
officials still expressed faint hopes
for the ships safety.


NO WRECKAGE FOUND


They pointed out the Army
transport Meigs, which found the
oil spot, had radioed the oil film
was fading away rapidly when
last sighted. This, they declared,
indicated there was no wreck
underneath it.


The hunt today centered be-
tween the oil spot and the coast
of Southern Luzon Island. The
MeigS and four Navy destroyers
were zig-zagging slowly westward
from where the ominous oil was
found. Other warships and six
Army planes secured the ocean
area south of Samar Island, most
easterly of the Philippine Islands,
while four Navy amphibians and
private aircraft combed island
Shorelines.


OIL TO BE TESTED


A sample of the oil was being
brought back to be examined more
closely in a laboratory.


The Bureau of Air Commerce
head investigator, Inspector I. Yu-
rovich, was due to arrive in San
Francisco from Washington, D. c.,
today and was expected to take the
next clipper Wednesday for Ma
Mia.


Regarding the rumors of sabo-
tage sweeping Manila and Wash
ington U. S. officials were silent.

Bitter fighting ragged north, south
and west of Shanghai today as
Chinese and Japanese forces
launched major offensives on
widely separated fronts.


The battles we're waged under
heart-breaking conditions as bitter
cold swept virtually the entire
country, most of which was blan-
keted by deep snow.

Pushing north from Nanking,
China's fallen capital. Japanese
troops launched a major drive up
| the Pukow-Tientsin railroad. Chi
nese reports from Hankow admit
ted the situation of Chinese de-
tenders along the railroad was

making headway.

battle was being fought near the
Port of Hangchow, which Japanese

in that region, however, are bit
terly contesting every foot of
ground they yield.

neSe legions unleashed a direct

despite a shattering barrage from
two japanese warships stationed
off Wuhu in the river, which at
tempted to relieve the pressure
against the Nipponese forces in
that area.


Japanese headquarters here
claimed another victory in North
China, stating Nipponese armored
tanks in a swift assault had cap
tured HohSien, in Anhwei prov
ince, near the Grand Canal and
vital Lunghai Railroad.

were meeting serious resistance.
Chinese regular army columns
were reported to have pierced the
Nipponese lines six miles west of

japanese reinforcements were

Who left the garden gate unlatched,


Who left the hosepipe the lawn,
Who used my favorite pen, who scratched
My desk, who starts from early morn
The radio screechng, who explores


The kitchen larder, lets the bath
Run over, rushes out of doors,


Haf-naked down the garden path,
Indifferent to the bitter weather -
Who sewed my trouser legs together?
Whose shoes are these with laces knotted,
Whose shorts are these flung anyhow,
Whose shirt is this with jam stains spotted?
Young villain, have caught you now!
But just too late since you are sleeping,
Your head pressed deep in the white pillow,
Your brown throat from your jacket peeping,
Your hair like gold, tumbling billow:
Is this the boy must accuse
OF putting tin-tacks in my shoes?
Whose laughter rings through all the house,
Who always has new cut bleeding
Who can be quiet mouse


When gainst my knee, as am reading,
A fair head leans? Who, with kiss,


Impulsive, sweet as April rain,
Will some haf-risen doubt dismiss


And lead me captive in his train?
Let all my years count up their treasure,
This bov love outweighs their measure.

CANTON, China, June 16.-An OIL
cial proclamation that six japanese
bombing planes attempting an attack
on the Canton area had been shot down
today started joyous celebrations in
this rnuch-bombed city.


The announcement, BY the local gov
ernment, asserted Chinese pursuit
planes met and defeated the invaders.
Canton's remaining populace, which
has suffered death-dealing Japanese
air attacks almost without respite for
three weeks, received the news ecstati-
cally.

again bombed the railway north of
Canton, after which 13 Chinese pur-
suit planes set out and caught them
at Lokchonghsien, about 200 miles
north of the city near the border be-
tween Kwangtung and Human prov
inces.


The Chinese planes then flew rings
around the slow-moving death en-
gines," said the proclamation, ma
chine-gunning and shooting down the
bombers one by one"


The Japanese in bombing the rail-
way were attempting to block the
northward shipment of munitions.


Hitherto japanese air raiders have
met no real resistance over Canton,
and the unexpected Chinese defense
strengthened reports that the Chinese
high command had sent 80 French
made planes to the Canton area since
the present series of japanese bomb
ings began May %.

NEW YORK, July 2-Commodity
prices swung in sharply divergent arcs
this week; industry's raw materials
soaring on heavy demand. while grains
and foods declined further.
The two-week boom in security
prices-one OF the most spectacular
in history-stimulated speculation in
staples that would benefit quickly
from increased industrial activity.
The ferrous metals-tin. lead,
zinc and copper-were all substantially
higher on the week, with sales running
far ahead of any comparable period
since last fall.


Steel scrap continued buoyant in
major consuming centers. Rubber
was actively bid for at Is cents a
pound, cents above the low Of two
months ago. Hides jumped a full
cent to 10 cents pound as shoe pro-
duction mounted and available stocks
Of hides dwindled.


Textiles moved ahead for the fourth
consecutive week Cotton cloth busi-
ness reached record proportions. ac-
cording to trade reports, and prices
were almost 10 per cent above mid
June levels. Bare shelves of most
retailers and many wholesalers, plus
signs the market was ready to turn
around. released the deluge OF orders
Silk was also higher, although wool
dipped moderately.


Other Staples Ease.


Other industrial staples, however,
weakened. Quotations for steel bill
lets were cut for the first time since
1882 in an effort by the steel trade
to increase business. Lumber, turpen-
tine and bituminous coal also gave
ground


Grains declined for the second week
to within a fraction of the years low
point. This was taken by the trade
to mean rust and other pestilential
damage to crops was smaller than
anticipated a fortnight back Corn,
wheat and oats shared the weakness


Cotton, however, shot above 8 cents
a pound for the first time in more
than two months The steady up
ward trend Of mill operations recently
and the prospect of better business
ahead was a potent factor in the
bulge.


Food prices were mixed, although
important staples like eggs. flour and
butter tilted downward Sugar, cocoa
and lard turned up slightly. Hogs and
lambs also bettered somewhat.

PRINCE FREDERICK, Md,
July 1.-Two 18-year-old girls
and a24-year-old youth today
stood in the shadow Of the gal
lows, charged with the murder Of
William Warrent Can't, SIS,
wealthy Port Republic farmer.


The trio, Betty Bierer, Margaret
Abel and Walter Stinnett, proba-
bly, will be arraigned on the charge
before Justice Of the Peace w. w.
Duke here tomorrow and held
without bond for action OF the
November term Of the grand jury.
KILLING ADMITTED


All three have admitted the
killing, officials said, but the girls
assert Stinnett fired the fatal
shots, while the youth says the
Bierer girl did the shooting.


All three admit that after they
killed the elderly farmer they
robbed him, stole his car and fled.
They abandoned the car near In
dian Head, stole a boat and rowed
across the Potomac to Fairview
Beach, Va, where they were ar
rested yesterday.


Indicating that he will seek the
death penalty for the trio, States
Attorney Arthur w. Dowell said
today:


I'VE have a strong case
against them. There is no ques-
tion about an accidental shoot
ing. We have evidence to show
this was a case of deliberate
murde rand robbery, and we
shall ask the full penalty Of the
law.


ALL THREE INVOLVED
"All three are equally involved
In this killing, and we have a
good idea who did the shooting.
But all are involved and all will
face the same penalty"

Raymond Abel, oca farmer, and
mother Of q S-year-od child, ad-
mttted the trio had planned to

money with him.


Stinnett used Gantt'S own gun
and fired the fatal shots, she told

Clared the shooting was accidental
and climaxed drinking party.


r ADMITS ROBBERY

$249, then took his car and fled.
They were arrested after they had

and a Storekeeper became Suspi-
ciouS and called police.

turned to Washington from Fred
erickSburg, and questioned by

Deputy Coroner, who worked with

Esther Lewis murder case last
month.

taken to Baltimore and held in the

Great Britain and France. facing a
crisis in Europe, are making every

plane re-enforcements they have or
dered in the United States.

partment officials. Should conflict

American Aviation Corp. France has

tiss-Wright.


France preceded Britain, through

plants.

The Department OF Agriculture has
announced the designation of four agri-
cultural research areas in which labora-
tories are to be established under the
new Farm Act. The laboratories, for
which s4,000000 was allotted, are to
make studies Of the products in each
area.


For decades the Department of Agri-
culture has done valuable work, on
national scale, in the sciences upon
which agriculture depends. The State
agricultural colleges and other institu-
tions have carried on similar work upon
more localized lines. The new labora-
tories will have the effect of combining
the best features Of both national and
local studies.


The laboratory for the Eastern area,
which includes Maryland and Virginia
will confine it's studies at first to to-
bacco, apples, potatoes, milk and vege-
tables.


The step is another toward the proper
solution of the farm problem. Crop
control benefits and the like help only
temporarily. Better results will come
when the farmer can devote his labor
to producing crops for which utilization
studies have demonstrated a demand,
and from which scientific work has elm
mated waste.

BY the Associated Press.


LONDON, March 26.-The United
States proposal that European and

While reports from Vienna told Of
several thousand Austrians - mostly
Jews-storming the United States con-

liminary survey of reaction to the
United States relief proposal indicated
that Europe's liberal and democratic
nations favored the proposal and that
no obstacle to carrying it out had been
encountered officially SO far.


Britain Will Help.


The British government promised to
give its immediate attention to the
proposal. which Secretary Hull dis
patched to nine European governments
and all of the American republics.


The French press gave prominent
display to the story and the govern
ment said 1t would send Secretary
Hull favorable reply soon.


Switzerland was counted among the
most interested countries because Aus
trian refugees have been pouring across
Its borders for days.


Scandinavian countries gave sympa-
thetic attention to the United States
suggestion.


In Brussels, officials declared Bel
gium was ready to cooperate fully
with the United States in forming an
international committee to help solve
the problem.


Italy Remains Silent.


italy, however. remained silent and
nothing officially was heard about
Secretary Hull's suggestion in Austria.
Germany ignored it. since Reichs-
fuehrer Hitler's government was not
made party to the proposal.


The Italian public learned Of the
proposal through a dispatch distributed
by the Italian official news agency,
which said President Roosevelt and

British. American and French news

SHANGHAI. April 16. japanese

offensive in their stalemated Shan
tung drive.


One was a rigid censorship they
clamped on all dispatches dealing with
military and shipping activities on
the North Shantung coast.


Another was the movement Of REIN
forcements down the coast toward
TalerhchWang. where the japanese
suffered their most disastrous defeat
OF the nine-month-old war last week.


Troops Near Chuhsien.


These troops were reported between
Chuhsien and Jihcao, so miles north
of Lini on the South Shantung front,
where the war has been begged down
for month


These developments came as reports
persisted in Toxic that Premier Prince
Fumimaro Konoye was considering re-
signing because of disagreement with
army and navy officials over conduct

an elaborate demonstration OF Japa-
neSe military strength soon may be
given as the imperial army, blocked in

Railway, pushes through Eastern
Shantung in new drive on battered
Taierhchwang.

constructing strong defense works

cials, charging they had been unable

BY the Associated Press.


SHANGHAI, March 20 Sunday -
A japanese Army estimated at $50 900
men smashed forward on the southern
Shantung front today in an offensive,
some foreign military observers con-
sidered, the most extensive battle since
the World War.


Backed by heavy compliments of
artillery. planes and tanks, the Jap
anese pushed from the north as ap-
proximately 250,000 Chinese sought to
stem the advance Casualties were
heavy on both sides Of the Central
China fighting.


Approaching Suchow. .


japanese reported they were within
striking distance of their main objec-
tive, Suchow, where Chinas main
east-west Lunghai and north-south
Tientsin-Pukow railways cross.


japanese aerial scouts said Chinese
defending Suchow were fleeing in dis
order under continuous plane bonn
bardment.


Chinese reported their forces
launched successful counter-a attacks
on the Tientsin- Pukow line, where
5000 japanese were killed. Foreign
advices indicated, however, that the
japanese were advancing steadily
along the north-south railway.


Japan's strategy seemed to foreign
military observers now to call for cap
ture of Suchow by the troops driving
south, which then would join strong
japanese forces moving up from Peng-
pu. From Suchow the combined
armies would strike west along the
Lunghai to Chengchow, thus eliminat-
ing the dangerous crossing of the
Yellow River, which would be neces-
sary if drive on Chengchow came
from the north.


Hankow Next Objective.


From Chengchow, junction of the
Lunghai and the Peiping- -Hankow
railways, the japanese would thrust
south toward Hankow, China's tenn
porary capital


simultaneously with the thrust
from Chengchow other would move
west from Wuhu to attack Hankow.
In the Japanese march through
Southern Shantung important coal
mines fell into their control yesterday
at Tsoachwang, 180 miles northwest
of Marking.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla, March 1s.-
Coast Guard Division headquarters
said today three of its ships and one
of its planes had failed to locate the
British motorship Princess Pat, which
was reported drifting helplessly in the
Atlantic Ocean about 100 miles east
southeast of here.


The 1l2-foot freighter, with a crew
of eight and cargo of lumber, left
here Wednesday for Guadeloupe. Late
Thursday the S. S. Mosil radioed the
Coast Guard it had sighted the Prin-
cess Pat drifting at sea with a broken
tailshaft. The Princess Pat does not
have radio.


The Coast Guard boats Vigilant,
Pandora and Colfax and plane from
the Charleston base have been unable
to locate the disabled freighter.

SHANGHAI, March 13 Sunday -
Chinese said today they had averted
a threatened Japanese drive into
Shensi Province, China's Communist
stronghold, by recapturing two i'm
portant towns on the Yellow River


One Of these was Hoku, from which
the Japanese reported yesterday they
had started fanwise move across the
northern end Of Shensi. The other
was nearby Paoteh.


River Crossing Denied.


The Chinese insisted that the jap
anese had not gained a foothold in
Shensi. They said they had repulsed
a Japanese attempt to cross the Yellow
River and enter the province at
Hancheng, about rs miles north OF the
rivers big bend" where the Japanese
were trying to cross and cut the
Lunghai Railway


Near the big bend" the japanese
continued to shell Tungkwan, Lunghai
railway city and gateway to southern
Shensi. They also bombarded Wen-
slang. q short distance to the east
on the south bank Of the river.


Battle on Yangtze River.


A battle between Chinese guerilla
troops and Japanese gunboat was
reported at Hohsien. Yangtze River
town, near where the United States
gunboat Panay was bombed and sunk
by Japanese last December.


The Japanese said they captured
700 Chinese and took 20 junks loaded
with 10000 bags of salt.


Two japanese merchants, kidnapped
by Chinese bandits yesterday near
Kashing. so miles southwest of
Shanghai, were released today upon
payment Of $4,000 ransom.

Coach Carl F. Heintel at Woodrow
Wilson has a tougher job on his

BY the Associated Press.


BARCELONA, Nov. 24.-Nine
swift insurgent bombers dumped
new death into Barcelona's streets
this morning in the eighth raid in
% hours.


The number of dead was not
established at once. The toll for
the previous seven raids yesterday
and during the night was 48 dead
and 148 wounded.


Heavy Anti-Aircraft Fire.


Coming from the north in two
squadrons at 9:45 am, the bombers
weaved warily across the city against
heavy anti aircraft fire. After
bombing several sections. they
wheeled away toward the Mediter-
ranean.


Government pursuit ships had
patrolled the starlit, moonless
Barcelona skies all night long and
twice fought with invading bombers.
One bomber was reported shot down.


The drumming of the plane mo-
tors and the rattling of gunflre were
audible over the whole city, but
nocturnal watchers could make out
few details of the fights.


SearchliEhts Kept on.


The city's searchlights were kept
of most of the time to avoid giving
away positions of government
planes.


Occasionally a stream of white
tracers spat across the sky from
government chaser. This was
answered after a few minutes by
red streak of insurgent tracer bullets.


Then motors whined high and
low, as the planes twisted about into
new positions.

through snow and intense anti-air-

warplanes today raided Sian, capital
of Shensi Province, in Northwest
China.


The Japanese reported the de-
struction of many important Chinese
government buildings. They said a
hail of bombs through the snow
blasted military and Communist
headquarters in the center of the city
and caused numerous fires.

During the past few days the Jap
anese have redoubled their efforts
to wipe out remnants of the Chinese
air force, bombing Sian, Lanchow
and other known airfields.

reports the Human provincial cap

fire, with heavy damage to Amer
lean mission property.


The Anslo-American China Inland
Mission. the Hudson Taylor Hos
pital and the American Evangelical
Mission Church. all within the
walled city, were reported destroyed.
Persons connected with the insti-
tutions were said to be safe.

japanese aerial observers reported

NEW YORK, Jan. 29.-The sands
of Treasure Island are getting too hot
today for the pirates of big business.


Chests filled with their loot still
wash ashore on the rising tide. but
the thieves who smuggle merchandise
to undersell competitors are beginning
to shift their feet in dire distress.

again."


The cables are right. The customs
men are pinching off the United
States supply of smuggled diamonds,
dope, watch parts. fancy clothes and
even human beings. History's biggest
pirate bands are being smashed.


The profits were immense in the
case of diamond smugglers, pirates
who had false bottoms in their treas
ure chests and used the fastest ocean
liners as ferry boats.


This is their story:


The shores of Manhattan had been
the sands of Treasure Island to the
gem buccaneers for decades. A mil
lion dollars worth of cut-price stones
flooded the Maiden Lane markets each
year. The customs men knew it.
They knew the dealers who were I'M

and searched their baggage carefully
every time the dealers came home
from abroad. But they found no
gems.

searched for clue to the big ring.
They knew when and where the dia-

find them.

JERUSALEM, Aug. 20.-Troops
planes and police searched the hills
around Hebron today for band which
raided and terrified that city of $4,000

clay's Bank, destroyed an armored

the gang fled to the hills


Authorities clamped down a 24-hour
curfew on Hebron at dawn, and the
situation was normal again today.


Arplanes sought out the positions of
organized bands and reported them to
army headquarters. Authorities sent
heavy reinforcements into the terror
lied northern sections, trying to drive
the bands into pocket along the
Syrian border.

thought finessed, whereupon West
spread his hand, setting the contract

swings in evidence.

steels, motors and assorted favorites 4
fast whirl. The ticker tape, for a

Even with the expansion of volume
at the finish, transfers failed to reach
900, 900 shares.


Near StandstiM at Noon.

parade of Flyer Howard Hughes and

In business in those months, still

ington authorities and from further
signs that the Governments pump
printing program was beginning to
take hold. Brokerage sentiment was
propped by the resistance exhibited
by stocks generally after last-hour
relapses in the past two sessions.

PRAHA, Czechoslovakia. March 10.
Diplomatic sources, today asserted
Adolf Hitler had demanded that
Czechoslovakia renounce her military
alliance with Soviet Russia as the
price of peace with Germany.


The demand, said to have been con-
veyed to President Eduard Benes
through diplomatic channels, was re-
| ported as the Czech government con-
formed with other German demands
and gave the 3,500,000 Germans within
her borders greater voice in their gov
ernment.


End of the Russian alliance was said

talks to lessen Czech German fric-
ton.


Informed persons said it was being
made increasingly clear to Benes and
Premier Milan Hodza that locked
| Czechoslovakia, two-thirds surrounded
by an expanding Germany, must be-
come a satellite of Nazi Germany to
avoid war.


To do this she must sever her MILL

manyS economic order

cred that only thus could the Czechs
and Slovaks retain their political and
cultural independence won in the
World War peace treaties.

That's news, wonderfully good news, in

the nesting grounds and the feeding marshes

heart again after period when they all but
despaired, and when the talk was going
around that sooner or later the Federal gov
ernment would have to decree an absolutely
closed season for an indefinite number of
years.

place?

ernment Of Premier william Aberhart
in Alberta Province.


The court not only ruled unconsti-
tutional three Alberta bills bolstering
the social credit program. but Chief
Justice Lyman Duff ruled against the
Alberta social credit act. the corner
stone of the Aberhart governments
financial structure.


Going outside the points specifically
referred to the court, Chief Justice
Duff handed down an opinion that the
social credit act was outside the legal
Jurisdiction of the province.


The opinion was considered highly
important, because 1t threw doubt on
the validity of the whole effort of the
Aberhart government, which came into
power in Alberta in 1885, to set up a
new economic scheme for the province


The three bills ruled unconstitu-
tional were the credit regulation bill,
ito amend and consolidate the credit
of Alberta regulation act; the Alberta
press bill, Ito ensure the publication
of accurate news and information.
and the bill increasing taxes on banks
in Alberta.


The Supreme Court also ruled that
the Dominion government had power
to disallow provincial legislation, and
that a lieutenant governor had the
right to reserve provincial legislation
until the Governor General of Canada
had indicated his approval or disap-
proval thereof.

VIENNA. March 5.-Police were
summoned today to halt riot between
swastika- wearing Nazi students and
government supporters at Vienna Uni
versity.

regular Saturday meeting of fraterni-

government supporters countered with
rousing "heil Schuschnigg!" and the

munists while the youth involved de-
clared the NaZis were responsible. The
official version said that only non-
political jealousies of rival boy groups

er, Hans Lalitsch. was said by physi-
clans to have been fatally wounded
when he refused to raise his hands at
the order Of 10 masked men who in
vaded an Austrian youth movement
hall. After shooting the teacher and
16-year-old boy the masked raiders
escaped in automobiles.

Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg has
gained powerful support from the Aus
trian Socialists in his fight to prevent
the illegal spread Of nazism.


The chancellor received a delegation
of Socialist workers today One private
news agency reported the reconcilia-

NEW YORK. July 2.-Fresh buying
fuel steamed up the stock market to-

climbed as much as four points.


Exceptionally large overnight pur-

rooms at the start. Blocks of 900 to

The pace slowed later and prices

ness with which offerings were abb

port and the list pushed up to the

ous traders cancelled plans to get an

side from all parts of the country, but

The 10 Camp Fire Girls meeting
for three-day convention here were
having the time of their young lives
today. their schedule including tea
with Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt,
visit to Congress and breakfast in
the Senate dining room.


The youngsters, garbed in white
MILDLY blouses, red ties and dark
skirts and wearing arm bands with
the cross logs and flame insignia,
were entertained by Senator Hattie
Caraway of Arkansas at breakfast.
They presented bright smiles and
much tossing of pig tails and curls
to the Senators who dropped in to
say hello to their young constituents.


Senator Lonergan of Connecticut
was applauded when he greeted the
girls with their own password "Wo-
hello" which stands for work, health
and love. He urged the girls to keep up
with their work, even when they left
the Camp Fire group. and stressed the
need for conservation of wild life and
natural resources.


Senator Gillette of Iowa, after break
fasting with the youngsters, took a
way between the Capitol and the
Senate Office Building. Representa-
tive Honeyman of Oregon also spoke
briefly.


The girls were to have tea with
Mrs. Roosevelt at pm. after being
shown through the White House gar
den. This evening they will have
rally meeting in the south auditorium
of the Department of Agriculture and
will be given a preview of Conserva-
ton Service movies. Raymond Evans
of the Agricultural Extension Service
will welcome them.


Enjoy Box Luncheon.


More than 100 Camp Fire Girls,
Including 40 from Washington and
Bethesda, Md, made themselves at
home in Rock Creek Park yesterday
and settled down to box lunches
amid trees typical of the ones they
have worked to conserve.


They wandered along the creek
behind the Joaquin Miller cabin,
around which the luncheon tables
were set, and investigated the swings
and examined the 20 trees they had
sent to Rock Creek Park as a lasting
memory of their rally. Mrs Arthur
H. Vandenberg, wife of the Michigan
Senator, carried boxes of doughnuts
from table to table. She is vice
chairman of the national conserva-
ton project of the Camp Fire Girls
and summoned the girls to Washing
ton for the convention.


After the picnic the girls gathered
for the ee-plantlng ceremony. Mrs.
Vandenberg read the inscription to
be put on the bronze memorial marker
at the foot of the gum tree. which
was sent by the Cleveland. Ohio,
girls. The Cleveland delegation was
the largest at the rally.


Finnan Welcomes Girls.


&C Marshall Finnan. superintendent
Of National Capital Parks. accepted
the trees for the United States and
Welcomed the girls. Edward Kelley,
administrative assistant, pointed out
that Rock Greek Park was good
example of conservation and said it
was appropriate that the Camp Fire
Girls, who are young conservationistS,
were celebrating in the park.


-Four Camp Fire Girls joined in
spadlng dirt into the ground around
the gum tree. 1t was explained that
the spade used in the ceremony had
been used in breaking ground at
every important ceremony in Wash
ington and the vicinity for 40 years.
First used by President Theodore
Roosevelt, the spade has figured in
the ground-breaking ceremonies at
the Lincoln Memorial and the Tomb
of the Unknown Soldier and has
been held by every President since.


The girls who spoke briefly at the
ceremony included Miss Mary Jane
Anderson of Bethesda. Miss Beatrice
Pugsley, Buffalo, N. Y; Miss June
Wamble. Walla Walla, Wash, and
Miss Lorraine Sterkel, Cleveland.


Visit Pierce Mill.


Before the girls left Rock Greek
Park they visited Pierce Mill and saw
the old mill wheel turn. In the eve
ming they held a swap party" to
discuss the conservation problems in
their own regions.


The delegates represent 250O00
girls. Those attending from Wash
ington and Bethesda include Miss
Lucille Harrell, Miss Marguerite
Schaffer, Miss Anderson and Miss
June Slaughter. Chaperons for the
local delegates are Mrs Elinor c.
Hearn and Mrs. Paul Ledig.

LIMA, Dec. 3l.-What were the
real achievements of the eighth Pan.
American Conference and what
concrete results will come out Of the
maze of resolutions and declarations
pushed through during the 10 days
OF the conference? 49,.


These were questions which states
men from the 81 American repub-
lies were asking themselves today
as they moved homeward to face
the new year.


And when they find the answer,
they probably will conclude the best
results were not tangible things that
were put into documents but rather
Intangible things.


Among the intangibles must be
counted, as far as most of the re-
publics and particularly the United
States are concerned, the debate and
argument that surrounded the flght
over the continental solidarity"
declaration.


Certainly this debate was more
potent than the rather weak dec
laratlon that was finally approved
by the conference. i.


1t was generally agreed, although
the United States professed salts
faction, that the final declaration
did little to combat the thing the
whole movement was aimed at
propaganda efforts of certain Euro
pean nations in Latin America.


On the other hand, the debate
dragged the propaganda problem
into the open and acquainted the
world with the fact that the United
States and many other nations were
alarmed over the subtle work which
the European propagandists had
been carrying on In Latin America
for the past five year.


Another intangible that had a real
value was the willingness Of almost
all the delegates to work on q give
and-take basis. Only on one issue
did the delegates show signs of Stub
bornness and that was the 'conti-
mental solidarity" declaration.
