FORT MEADE, Md, Sept. 20.
Despite storm and rain the bri-
gade maneuvers of the Third
Corps Area continued here today.


In conditions reminiscent of
war days in France, infantry and
cavalry plowed through the mud
while batteries of field artillery
and tanks found the going diff
cult.


The troops were thrown out to-
day in the most important phase
of the maneuvers, brigade move
ments with all branches of the
service coordinating.


TARGET PRACTICE


Following this major maneuver,
the troops will return to their
home posts, while reports of the
umpires will be studied by Off
GERS to determine the effective
ness of the troop movements.


The Third Cavalry and Six
teenth Field Artillery from Fort
Myer will remain at Fort Meade
for several days after the maneu-
vers end, firing on the target
ranges.


The maneuvers this year, the
most intensive ever held, have
brought all the latest developments
of the Army into the field.


MOBILE FORTS


While the cavalry still clings to
the horse, the regiment has been
semimotorized, having a number
of armored cars attached to it.


These cars are mobile forts,
armed with heavy and light ma
chine guns. antitank guns, and
equipped with radio so they can
keep in touch with regimental
headquarters at all times, giving
information of enemy" troop
movements.

GREENBELT, Md. Nov. 24.-The
Greenbelt Town Council has ap-

this model low-cost housing COM

given an opportunity to record their
suggestions as to what the building
should contain.


Under present plans the building
will house bowling alleys, a gymna-
stun, reading rooms, billiard room,
table tennis rooms and several meet
ing rooms. The town is now using
the elementary school building as
community hall.


It was announced that r. j..
Wadsworth, architect for the Green
belt project, and Hale Walker, the
original Greenbelt planner, have
offered their services free for the
planning of the new building.

aneSe troops stalled temporarily al

Plan to Occupy Chengchow.


The japanese plan has been to oc-

through the Chinese ring.

push to the west along the vital
Lunghai line.

feng, had been captured. japanese
said then that Chinese were beginning
to fall back from the Lunghai area.

reports, the japanese military spokes-
man here said he lacked confirmation,
but said such advances were quite
likely as events are happening fast
along the Lunghai now"

Japanese occupied highways both
south and southwest of Kaifeng.


Railway Reported Cut.


The reports by way of Hankow said
japanese forces south of the Lunghai
had pushed spearhead westward and
cut the Peiping Hankow Railway,
occupying Yencheng, midway between
Hankow and Chengchow

no information on the reported Lung
hal developments, but said they be-
lieved the reported Japanese occupa-
ton of Kaifeng possibly was correct
since the invaders had been threaten

A japanese naval spokesman mean

: SHANGHAI, July 7.-Terrorist at
lacks against Japanese resumed In
Shanghai today on the first ami
fersary OF the China War.


: Foreign troops, including United
States marines, and police reserves in
ensified their patrol Of sultry streets


p guard the International Settlement
Ind the French Concession.


Four were killed and Ave wounded
6y bombs, grenades and bullets. Two
Of the dead were Japanese and two
we're Chinese. A British colonial SOL
der was injured


There were hurries of machine gun
Are in outlying districts and reports
ef sporadic shooting in industrial
pootung, across the Whangpoo River
from Shanghai proper, that may have
meant a new series of attacks by
Chinese guerrilla units.


Outbreaks Frequent.


There had been similar outbreaks
Once the Japanese established con-
troll of Shanghai and drove the
Chinese toward Marking last No
fember g.


For the most part, however. out
Yard order prevailed here while the
battle front was carried beyond Nam
Hing, further into the interior in the
present drive along the Yangtze River
b reach Hankow, China's provisional
capital.


;. The Chinese and Japanies armies
now are in a near deadlock along the
Yangtze about Hukow and Kiukiang,
l6O miles from Hankow and $50 miles
from Shanghai.


How much longer the war may last
still is q question that one cannot
shswer.


Numerous Peace Feelers.


> There have been numerous peace
feelers since efforts toward mediation
were attributed last fall to the German
Ambassador, Oskar Trautmann, since
recalled.


Behind-the-scenes efforts still are
icing made, but thus far all have
failed because neither the Chinese nor
Japanese have sustained overwhelm-
ing victory or disastrous defeat, and
both still are determined to prolong
the struggle rather than quit with a
lpss of face.


I The Chinese persistently have been
pushed back into the interior until the
Japanese soon may be within striking
distance of Hankow. But the Chinese
high command successfully has avoid
ed decisive frontal battle.


The army's policy has been to de-
lay the japanese as long as possible. to
cause great damage and then with
draw to new defense positions
Chinese guerrilla units constantly are
attacking from the rear to make diff
cult japanese occupation of territory.


Reports from Peiping tell Of in
creasing numbers Of these guerrillas
and Communist troops, causing seven
of that city's 13 massive gates to be
kept closed.


Peiping, with its government of
elderly Chinese under Japanese pro-
lection, celebrated the anniversary
with champagne, saki and beer-but
with the entire available force of Chi
Hese police, secret agents and Japa-
nese gendarmes on guard against dis
order.


Generalissimo Chang Kai-shek,

nese people to halt the madness of

man officials persisted in denying
any extraordinary moves. But it
was learned on good authority

BY the Associated Press.


The Justice Department agreed yes
terday to confer with officials of the
National Retail Credit Association on
the advisibility of modifying a decree
regulating certain activities of the
association.


The conferences will begin next
week.


Attorneys for the organization al
ready have told the department that
the decree, entered in the Eastern
Federal District Court of Missouri in
1888, stands as cloud upon activi-
ties Of association members. They
denied that the association violated
any antitrust statute by withholding
credit information from members.


The present decree-filed after the
Government charged the association
with violating the Sherman Anti Trust
Act-enjoined the organization from
dividing territory exclusively among
its membership and from discrim-
mating against non-members in the
sale of credit information.

Already ravished by storms

the Atlantic Coast line today pre-
pared itself against a new storm
moving in from the ocean with
increasing density.


Washington will feel little Of
this except perhaps more rain and
strong winds, but storm warnings
were posted in nearby Chesapeake
Bay, and small craft advised to
seek shelter.


Northeast gales are sweeping
along the Virginia Capes and off
the coast of Maryland and Della
ware.


GALE AT ATLANTIC CITY


At Atlantic City, the storm which
is sweeping up from about 100
miles off the Maryland coast had
reached gale proportions this
morning and was heading toward
New York with slowly increasing
intensity. The storms center is ex-
pected to pass near by east of
Nantucket late this afternoon or
early tonight.


WIND WILL DROP


The northeast gales along the
coast will back to north and
northwest and diminish, and the
northeast or eaSterly gales along
the southern New England coast
will back to north and northwest,
and also diminish. Along the
northern New England coast the
same condition is forecast.


New York is feeling the storm
heavily and is lashed with rains,
but there is no possibility, the
Weather Bureau says. of a repeti-
ton of last weeks gale.

Wholesale commodity prices regis

81 was 74.7. compared with 744 in

as 100 The index is now at the same

lower than year ago.


The increase in the all-commodity
index was largely due to higher prices
for farm products and foods and more
specifically to livestock and meats.
The index representing the prices of
all commodities except farm products
and foods showed a slight decline,
reaching new low point for the cur
rent recession.


In the food group about as many
items declined as advanced, but
marked upturns in meat prices re-
suited in the group index advancing
for the third consecutive week.


Cotton and grains were lower dur
ing the week, with wheat prices fall
ing to the lowest point reached since
1884.


Advances in prices of livestock,
however, were sufficient to raise the
farm product group average. Frac-
tional increases also took place in the
indexes of farm machinery and mis-
cellaneous commodities. Five of the
principal group indexes declined dur
ing the week, the largest recession
being in the metal price average.


Copper quotations were sharply
lower and smaller declines occurred
in steel scrap and tin. There was
also relatively large decline in the
chemical and drug index while the
building material, fertilizer material
and fertilizer indexes fell off only
slightly.

To the Editor Of The Star:


Recently attended one of our better
neighborhood theaters. Before the main
program began a picture of the flag of
the United States was flashed on the
screen and "The Star Spangled Banner"
was played. Even though the theater
was well filled, only few people stood
while the national anthem was being
played


This shows to what extent the Ameri-
can people have drifted from the things
the Stars and Stripes represent. We
have taken our liberty and freedom so
much for granted that we are becoming
careless of the very heart and core of
our lives.


With all the agitation from the
various "isms" now sweeping the country,
I would like to suggest that every thea
ter, at every performance, present the
American flag, together with some of.the
vital things it stands for. Maybe this
would help to make the American people
conscious once more of the wonderful
country they call home.


AN AMERICAN.

Alone, outside that closed and

DIR. Kent's in delivery. Any

She had left message for him;

alone with the grim night rou-

her, catching her for a moment
in its rhythm, then releasing her
to the sickening weight of her
own thoughts and fears.


The room in which she sat
opened upon the corridor, it's door
directly opposite the closed door
through which no one came
except once a hurrying inferno
who did not glance in Gloria'S
direction-who did not even seem
aware that she was waiting, had
been waiting, for one long hour.


DR. Carston had warned her that
it would be perhaps two hours
maybe longer. He had been
kind, as sympathetic as possible
for man whose traffic is forever
with suffering and pain.


WAITING


Waiting was intolerable. She
kept telling herself that the hos
pital had assured her that DR..
Carston, who was operating, was
the best in the city. She kept
telling herself that everything was
going to be all right. Tommy was
young and strong and would make
a desperate fight for life.


So there was nothing she could
do but wait wait for that wide
white door to swing open and then
search for an answer to her tor.
turing fears in the faces of the
doctors and nurses and operating
room attendants.


She got up from the low wicker
sofa, snapped off the light and
went to the window. She pulled
aside the thin cotton curtain. It
was dark and cold with stars that
seemed frosted against the black
drop of night.


She stood looking out at the
rear Of the hospital over the snow
covered roofs of stores bulked
dimly between her and the Palace
Hotel. And across the city, hardly
more than q towering shadow, was
Garfield Hospital and Peter. fight
ing grimly for some ones life as
DR.. Carston here was fighting for
Tommy's life.


She thought, IF Peter were only
here" And it occurred to her
suddenly that she had spent a
good many years wanting Peter
when she was in trouble.

CHICAGO, April SIN the records
Of boxing it will be related that Joe
Louis knocked out a certain Harry
Thomas in five rounds. Actually, and
by the rules of boxing Louis won in
three.


Late in the third round Louis drove
. terrific right to Thomas head that
sent the Minnesotan reeling in gro
tesque steps along the ropes, definitely
out. although still on his feet. Referee
Dave Miller sent Louis to his corner
and, turning to watch Thomas, heard
Nate Lewis, crafty manager of the ex-
engineer. shout, THE bells rung."
From the other corner came the clamor
Of Louis seconds, directing the cham
pion to complete his kill


The bell on the Chicago Stadium
ring is small and tinny and Miller,
thinking he might have missed the
gong, went to the opposite side of
the ring and asked Joe Triner, chair
man of the Illinois Boxing Commits
sion, if the round were over. Triner
shouted negatively and Miller turned
again toward Thomas.


Automatically Disqualified.


Old Nate Lewis, in the meantime,
had climbed into the ring and had
his man Harry seated on a stool.
Since the round was not over, Lewis
presence in the ring automatically
disqualified Thomas.


Miller contends he did not see Nate
Lewis push the stool into the ring
and Louis seconds did not imme-
diately protest, for they thought
Thomas was quitting. During the
tntermission Miller asked Louis to
continue for the sake of the spectators,
which he did without any risk, for
Thomas went down three times in the
fourth and twice in the fifth.


In his last two fights, Thomas had
been down II times-Schemeling hav-
ing dropped him six-and now is
qualified for membership in the ele-
vatormen's union.


Louis fought well enough for the
occasion, but there were observers who
believe he must be better against
Schmeling. Thomas awkwardly pat
termed his style after the German,
and, while the result was crude, STU
dents Of boxing form saw in the cham
pions defense weakness against such
right hands as Schmeling throws Louis
worked cautiously against Thomas
makeshift Schmeling style for two
rounds, but, after catching Harry wide
open in the third. reverted to his GUS
tomary pantherish fury.


Thomas Greatly Overmatched.


Thomas was greatly overmatched,
and, if he was leading Schmeli1g, six
rounds to two, when the fight was
stopped, the German must have been
very rusty, or gone back tremen-
dously. Thomas had little but stark
courage, but plenty of that. Few
would have survived Louis right-hand
blow in the third round or come up
four times to meet more paralyzing
punches. That jolt in the third
jerked my neck out a foot" Harry
ruefully admitted after the fight.


Louis is $16,659.65 nearer his first
million and now will go to Michigan
farm to continue light training for the
June match with Schmeling. Mean
time. Mike Jacobs will return to Chi
cago this week. to make survev of
Soldier Field, which makes it more
evident this city will be the scene of
the summer battle. Schmeling is
scheduled to arrive in the United
States April 30, and Jacobs will want
his plans we'll under way by that date.


Meanwhile, Chicagoans are wonder
ing if Uncle Mike had foresight when
he scheduled the Louis Thomas bout
for April Fools Day.

II wonderful sandy beaches Of

The New England mountains have
been pleasantly combined with other
natural resources in q way that makes
for the best in recreational advan-
tages. There are mountains in New
England that rise directly from the
sea. There are mountains that reach
skyward from the midst of forest
wilderness, stunting the huge timbers.
While necklaced by myriad-sized
lakes and punctuated by deeply chan
neled valleys, there are friendly peaks
whose submits share secrets with the
clouds.


While New England's mountains
may differ vastly in size and forma-
ton, they are all identical in two
aspects: Beauty and recreational op-
portunities. Rich green's intimately
blend with blues Of silver sheen. Lit
tie faky clouds float just above snow
crowned crests that rise from gray
crags above green slopes. Lovely
panoramas stretch for miles, display
ing the awe-inspiring wonders Of
nature.


ONE Of the best ways to thoroughly
~ enjoy the mountains Of New Eng
land Is to make q hiking tour or Q
horeback trip through them. Begin
ming in the White Mountains more
than q century ago, trail development
has gradually been extended through
out the six States to Q point where
close to 5000 miles Of hiking and bri-
die trails are constantly maintained
In class A condition. With such an
extensive network to choose from. it
will be easy for the visitor to find Just
the trail for his experience. Whether
one has several months or Just few
hours for hiking, there are trails for
his purpose.


A special favorite with New England
mixers is Mount Katahdin In North
ern Maine, q peak noted for its treeless
table-lands and precipitous cliffs.
Lakes encircle its feet. The great
Appalachian Trail continues from the
White Mountains through Maine to
this forest giant. Other principal
trails are reached from Millinocket on
the southeast and from Greenville on
Moosehead Lake. Mount Desert Island,
OF the Maine Coast, maintains q 400
mile trail system. -


Tho National Forest protects most
Of the White Mountains, where one of
the most extensive trail systems in the
world. constituting more than 1000
miles, awaits the hiker. Shelters and
huts, some with caretakers, dot the
region. The district centering about
Mount Washington Is Americas best
known tramping ground. OF the vari-
ous paths that ascend the mountain,
tho most popular Is the Tuckerman
Ravine Trail, starting At the Pinkham
Notch camp Of the Appalachian Noun
tain Club. North from Mount WASH
angton to the Canadian border Is q
vast region, heavily wooded, that con-
tains many lakes and isolated noun.
tains. Fine hiking centers In this
district exist at Chatham, Intervale
and Jackson.


Southwest Of Mount Washington is
franconia Notch where curious for
nations such as the Great Stone Face,

block of Columbia Rd. N. W., an

dismay, when she started to leave,

closed tightly.

Fire Department. Shortly fire
men arrived, placed scaling lad

the school door and rescued" the
teacher.

NEW YORK. April 19.-The year
old slump in stock prices. wiping out
more than half the value OF shares
listed on the New York Stock Ex-
change as Of March. 1887, affected
quotations in some industries substan-
TALLY more than others.


Stockholders OF concerns in the
leather business, for example, have
seen prices of their junior equities
chopped 70 per cent-measured by the
Standard Statistics Co. stock price
index-from the peak a year ago.


Holders Of gold mining shares, on
the other hand, have lost only per
cent in the face value Of investments


This bounds the extremes. Not q
single industry today boasts higher
stock values than last year, although
few months ago the ticker recorded
higher quotations for gold mining
companies than was the case in 1887


Cataloguing percentage changes in
the last IL months. based on the
statistical organizations indexes, shows
heavy industry to have been much
harder hit by the defiation than those
groups manufacturing goods for gen.
eral consumer use.


Register Greater Losses.


The six industries registering the
sharpest losses during the slump were
mostly capital goods producers. After
leather came railroads. with SO per
cent drop; paper producers, down 81
per cent: tires. 66 per cent; rail equip
ment and steel, 81 per cent; copper,
motors and air transportation, 81 per
cent.


Financial quarters explain the
greater er-than-average setback as the
result partly OF overoptimistic specu-
lation last spring and partly the fact
that, having passed the crest, demand
for capital goods dried up almost COM
pletely. This reversed the earnings
picture, replacing black ink with red
in many cases.


At the other end Of the roster,
among the industries suffering smallest
losses, were producers Of staples in
steady demand by the average individ-
ual, II gold is excepted.


Stocks in cigarette manufacturing
firms, for instance, were down 80 per
cent; textile fabricators dipped one
third: package food professors So per
cent and shoemakers 80 per cent.


Holding Firms Slump.


Utility operating companies showed
relatively moderate declines, with 4
dip Of 40 per cent. Holding concerns,
on the other hand. dropped S. per cent
from the peak last year. The diver.
gence, analysts point out, was caused
largely by the leverage factor inherent
in q holding company, based as it is
on equities Of other concerns, and
having either bonds or preferred stocks
with . prior claim on earnings stand
ing ahead Of the common stock.


Shares in firms dealing principally
with the Nations farmers recorded
almost identical declines from the
highs, mail order houses being knocked
down 81 per cent and agricultural ma
chinery manufacturers losing SO per
cent.


Airplane manufacturing, favored by
the Governments rearmament pro-
gram. receded IS per cent. This was
substantially less than the 81 per cent
loss In air transport stocks.

GREEN RIVER, Utah, June 30
Rainy weather aroused fears here to-
day for the safety of scientific expe-
dition of four men and two women
which set out 10 days ago to shoot
the dangerous canyons of the Colorado
River.


Veteran rivermen expressed concern
at recurrent storms of the past week,
In what is normally dry season.


Both the Green and the Colorado
are at flood stage now and these sud-
den mountain storms are going to
make the trip even more dangerous, :"
said one river rat"


The party, headed by Norman D.
Nevills, Utah riverman, and including
Miss Elzada Clover, Miss Louis Jotter
and Eugene Atkinson. University of
Michigan scientists; Don Harris of
the United States Geological Survey
and w. C. Gibson. San Francisco
artist photographer, set out down the
Green River June 20 in three light
boats, with boulder dam, 666 miles
southwestward, the goal.


First contact with civilization was
to be the halfway point of Lees Ferry,
Ariz. The party hoped to arrive there
July 4.


RRivermen believed the group now
was daring the Colorado River rapids,
one of the most dangerous laps.

HENDAYE. France (at the Spanish
frontier), July 23-Spanish govern
ment counter-attacks today further
slowed down the insurgent drive to-
ward Valencia while the two-year-old
Spanish war burst into new activity

madura and Catalonia.

push toward Valencia along the Ter
uel-Sagunto highway received 4 set

tured the village OF Terezuela, just

announced that the advanced right
wing Of the army famed out along
the road from Teruel had crossed into
Valencia Province nearly 40 miles
northwest of the provincial capital.


The governments armies in North
western Catalonia, near the French
frontier. attacked insurgent positions
around Sort, about 80 miles from
Barcelona. Insurgent reports said
lines remained unaltered.


On the Estremadura, or southwest
ern front, dormant for months, tnsur-
gent cavalrymen were said to have
dashed across a sparsely populated
plain in 20-mile advance to widen
the corridor between northern and
southern insurgent territory.

Container manufactures and

circles pointed out every pound of this

Auto Inventories Jump.

tally larger stocks last year END were

facturers.

WARSAW, Oct. 29 (P,.-Poland ar
rested about 1000 Germans in retalia
tory raids tonight. but orders for their
deportation to Germany were rescind-
ded hastily when Germany halted her
mass expulsion of Polish Jews.
Word from Berlin said the expulsions
had been stopped pending negotiations
Monday with Poland concerning the
status OF all Polish citizens residing in
Germany.


The Polish government, in the midst
OF attempts to persuade Germany to
halt the mass expulsion. asked local
ohcials to give Red Cross nurses and
the Polish Refugee Relief Committee
all possible assistance in obtaining food
and shelter for the deportees.


Samuel Wolpowitch, relief committee
chairman, reported that telephoned
advices from border points indicated
IL 900 Jews had crossed the border into
Poland by mid-morning. Other thou.
sands were being massed in trains and
concentration points at German Dor.
der stations.


Red Cross nurses and shipments OF
food were sent to the Polish Silesian
border zone where the situation wa.
most acute. Women and children wer.
among the refugees entering Silesia
Children were taken to orphanages anc
schools to protect them from a heavy
rain.


The Polish government. attempting
to keep the situation quiet. allowed
newspapers to publish only short &C.
counts. One paper was suppressed fol-
publishing foreign dispatch on the
deportations.

text:
LEES FERRY, Ariz., July 9
UN.S).-Undaunted and un-
shaken by their 18-day death-de-
flying journey down the Green
and Colorado Rivers, four men
and two women said today they
were ready to continue the expe-
dition to its ultimate destination,
Boulder Dam.


The party, feared missing for
several days, arrived here in
three boats late yesterday, tired,
tanned but with high morale,
They lost one boat in the Colorado,
Just after they left Green River,
but that didn't bother them.


AWAIT SUPPLIES


Refreshed after a good nights
sleep and fresh food, the six
adventurers said they we're ready
to start out again as soon as their
boats and supplies were refur-
bished.


In the party were DR.. Elzada
Glover, University of Michigan
botanist: Lois Jotter, her assist
ant; Eugene Atkinson, University
of Michigan zoologist; Don Harris,
United States Geological Survey
engineer; w. c. Gibson, San Fran
cisco Photographer, and Norman
D. NeVills, of Utah, veteran river
guide.


They left Green Hat, Utah, June
20 and had planned to reach Lees
Ferry, 300 miles distant, not later
than July 4. But they no sooner
set out than their troubles began.


BOAT CAPSIZED


Just after they turned into the
turbulent Colorado, the boat occu-
pied by Atkinson and Gibson over
turned in a swift whirlpool. Atkin-
son clung to the boat and was
swept downstream, while Gibson
swan to shore and was picked up
by one of the other boats.


Miss Clover and NevillS fought
desperately through several treach-

Atkinson and rescue him and re-
trieve the boat.


Miss Jotter, on shore during the
rescue, was forced to spend
chilly night alone, wondering what
had happened to her companions.
The next day, one of the boats
worked back up stream and took
her aboard.


FOOD OBTAINED


On July S, the party beached
and went ashore. They hiked to
Rainbow Natural Bridge, where
they replenished their food sup
plies from a cache left regularly

travellers.


On the morning of the sixth,

ferry.


On the trip, they saw three
Japanese gold miners operating
along the river before they got
into the steep-walled canyon. At
one portage they reported they
found an inscription made by the
Powell expedition in 1869.

PARIS, Nov. 7 Q.N.S0-A
17-year-old youth who sought re-
venge for the sufferings Of Jews
walked into the German embassy
today, suddenly drew a pistol and
critically wounded Ernst Won Rath,
the third secretary.


Asking for a high official-he
apparently bore no special malice
against Won Rath-the young
man cried:


IT want to take revenge on
you for the sufferings your fel-
low countrymen have caused
my fellow jews"


Wounds Serious


Overpowered by the embassy
staff and taken to Jail, the gun
man gave his name as Herschel
Seibel Grynsztan. He readily
confessed.


Wilhelm Legorka, embassy page,
who was present during the shoot
ing, expressed the opinion that
Johannes Welczeck, German am
bassacor, was the intended vic
tim.


Won Rath was hit twice. One
bullet lodged in the lung and
another in the liver.


At the fashionable clinic De
L'Alma, where Won Rath's condi-
tion was reported very bad" DR..
IBaumgartner operated on him in
an effort to save his life. The
wounded diplomats family was
summoned to his bedside.


The operation on Won Rath
lasted for two hours. Afterward,
DR.. Baumgartner said:


II cannot say until tonight
whether Won Rath will live or
die. His condition is extremely
critical. One bullet was re-
moved from his groin. The
other bullet in his left lung has
not been removed for the time
being"


Family Purge Victims


Grynsztan struggled to escape
when Won Rath's screams brought
the embassy staff to his side.


The youth mumbled brokenly to
police that he committed his act
because his own family was
among those suffering on the Ger
man-Polish border today.


The German embassy formally
requested the police to permit a
German government representa-
tive to be present during the ques-
tioning of the youth. The police
refused, whereupon embassy Off
cialS indicated they might make
a formal protest to the Quai dor
say.

By the Associated Press.


TIBERIAS, Palestine, Oct. g.
Nineteen Jews were killed by Arab
rebels today in one of the worst out
breaks in current Jewish-Arab rioting
over rival claims to Palestine as
homeland


Bodies Of those slain, about half of
whom were young children from l to
10 years old, were burned by the Arabs.
Two other Jews were injured seriously.


After cutting all telephone COM
munications, the Arab rebels entered
Tiberias from two directions. They
had occupied the surrounding hills
within stones throw of the Sea of
Galillee.


Suddenly a shrill whistle sounded.
1t was the signal for concerted at
tack on the Tiberias police station,
government Offices and British police
barracks.


Fires broke out in the Jewish syna-
gogue, the district commissioners
Offices and several houses.


Armed with rifles, bombs and dag
gers, the Arabs swooped down on
Jewish homes. They centered their
attack on three houses Six persons
were killed in one, five in another and
two in the third


The other Jews were killed in shoot
ings in different parts of the city.


Help came almost Immediately from
the trans-Jordan frontier force and
police stations Of neighboring settle
ment. Six Arabs were killed and the
remainder of the band was scattered.


Police said they might find addi-
tional massacre victims when debris of
burned houses is removed. Troops,
aircraft and bloodhounds searched the
whole Galillee district for the insur-
gents.

crossing.

pared line of defense on insurgent ad-
vance guards attempting to establish
bridgeheads.

ened, however, by lack of materials.

fell back, quantities of guns, tanks and
arms were left behind

front, from the Pyrenees on the French
border to the Mediterranean, has been
unchanged for several days: while
government resistance held firm in

flanks slowly forward

Another way is to place the plain

Cook chestnuts in boiling salted

When October sets the door ajar
for winters freezing winds and the
spotlight that has played on Europe's
summer travel pales the curtain call
is sounded on season that strikes
an exceptionally responsive chord in
the heart of every traveler-the winter
cruise season. OF late there has been
tendency to dramatize the Carlb-
beams tropics throughout the year,
upsetting the dubious decree that one
winter only. For the travel industry
has fortified itself with charts and
statistics on temperatures and the
constancy of ocean breezes to prove
that Jamaica in summer, for example,
is not an oven where eggs are baked
on the sidewalks. Still, winter remains
the season. for ports in the sun
and the magnet then shifts to pull
the vacation compass needle toward
the Caribbean, and beyond


Accustomed to shape its plans far in
advance, ship lines and travel agen-
cies have been releasing schedules of
short and long cruises from time to
time during the summer. In July
one could pick his ship for special
Christmas cruise to foreign islands
that lie off Americas Southern coasts.
The program was kept in the back
ground. however, until summer died
When the budgets, dented by summer
trips or swelled by stored-up ammuni-
ton for winter recreation, are smoothed
over or are about to pop, the ever
popular winter cruises will be brought
to the attention of all. But, nesting
down in his easy chair, inspired to
dream before an open fire, the Wash
ingtonian can begin to toy now plans
for a sun-ship holiday.

confirms. the impression that ship
lines have delayed the peak tempo of
sailings until chill weather has begun
to penetrate to the marrow of the
bones. But even now comfortable

de France, Curacao, Colon, Nassau,
Havana. to name few.

But the popularity of the short
cruise has done more than draw
name" ships from their Atlantic
courses. 1t has developed a regular
service, with some of the ships spe-
cially built for Caribbean waters;
not freighters, accepting a few pas
sengers as super cargo but vessels
giving the traveller excellent. even
sumptuouS accommodations. Famous
among these are the Grace Line ships
sailing weekly from New York and
the Great White Fleet, with sailings
on Wednesdays and Saturdays, all
touching Pan-American ports in their
Caribbean parade.


The Furness- Bermuda Lines Mon

might be called de luxe ferry service

Only four special cruises are listed

cruises, and the season is on!


Holiday cruises take the Spanish

and spread their figurative sails on
each of the seven seas. One of the
snappiest aristocrats of the cruise

one early January support cruise.
The Italian liner, Roma, the Gdynia-

couldn't actually be laughing and

ess with the ordeal of the dinner
staring her in the face.


The dinner began auspiciously, but
Isabelle was too overwrought to notice.
The soup was served, consumed and

from Mamie. Then behind her, Isabelle
heard the pantry door swing open.
The big moment had arrived. Mamie
was bringing in the fish - magnifi-
Gently whole. nestled in its garland of
parsley, sliced lemon and tomato.


"Well," Isabelle spoke with forced
brightness to Wally who sat at her
right, Il hope you think your wonder
full fish has been given the proper
attention" She turned her eyes to the
platter which Mamie had slipped in
between her and Wally.


Somehow she survived the shock of
what she saw: There was no large fish.
head, tail and all. The parsley was
there and the lemon and tomato -
surrounding broiled fish steaks.


''BoyT Wally helped himself to the

Isabelle made noise she meant for

The fish. the boys agreed. was the

what she was eating. She was too
furious to note that Mamie never once
spoke unless she was spoken to and
that she accepted with pleasant re-
serve the compliments heaped on her
cooking.


At last the dinner was over and
Isabelle led the way back to the living
room. As soon as she had, most
charmingly. seen that everyone was
comfortable she slipped away. She was
going to explode into a million pieces
if she didn't get into the kitchen!


To have to act the child in order to
get what was hers by right and then
not get it, was the final straw. Let
Mamie's feelings be hurt Other people
had feelings, too. Tonight Isabelle was
going to become grown-up even It
Mamie quit and went home forever.

shoes to her old slippers when Isabelle
swept in. She started to speak and
stopped. mouth agape at the sight of a
trout complete from eyes to tail, beau
tifully brown. lying in the open oven.


Why, this was the mystery of all
time! This was enough to drive a per-
son crazy.

book. You see that trout looking so
pretty on the outside? Just raw inside.
l was scared something like this was

Jonas Fields to bring me them BASES.

ate bass out of the river? Bass we

Samana Bay near the eastern end of
Santo Domingo.


A threatening storm sent the cruiser
Philadelphia with the President and
his party aboard into the shelter of
the Dominican bay early last night.

the Chief Executives good weather
luck and prevented fishing

anchor at 7 am. yesterday near Silver
Bank; but a southeasterly breeze
stirred the sea to such an extent that
plans were abandoned for exploring
the west side of the reef in small boats
or fishing for the first time since the
trip began at Charleston Saturday
morning.


Meanwhile, the Tanning skirted the
bank for several hours, continuing the
of1-course depth soundings that have
marked the trip since it started.


Then. at II am. the two vessels re-
sumed the trip leisurely, taking eight
hours to reach the shelter of Samana
Bay


The President spent a quiet day
dividing his time between his quarters
and the forecastle deck" said last
nights radio message to the navy
yard here.


"On the run down today monday

isting charts" it added.

A light was burning extra bright
in the Kurrie home for Christmas
morning.


1t outshone all the red and green
and blue lights on the Christmas
tree, was more brilliant than the
tinsel and gayer than the holly
trimmings.


The brightest light shone in the
face of Nancy Jean Kurrie.


You remember Nancy Jean. She's
the little Bethesda CMd.) girl who
couldn't live because an automobile
crash in July put out all but the
tiniest spark of life in her body
That would surely go out too, doctors
thought.


Went Home in October.


But it didn't. Nancy Jean re-
turned home in October.


She lived. And Saturday night
Santa Claus visited her home for
the fifth time. He must have known
OF her trying experience this year
for he brought her almost every
thing to make her happy.


Her face, now rosy and full
beamed when she saw the big doll
house, furnished with lights and all
She laughed with delight at q
funny-looking doll with a red nose
A big automobile, streamlined with
silvery wheels, made her blue eyes
open wide.


Nancy Jean is quite tomboy. 50
she was particularly pleased with a
small work bench with the little
hammer, saw and building materials
Other gifts filled the Kurrie living
room


Parents Share Happiness.


Oh, boy, I betcha it would take
me all day to count them!" the little
girl exclaimed as she went from one
present to another.


Her happiness was gloriouslv
shared by Mr.. and Mrs. Sebastian
M. Kurrie, her parents, who once
thought their only child would never
experience another Christmas.


Nancy Jean has been running and
playing with the other youngsters
in the neighborhood for nearly six
weeks now. She is strong again.
Her broken body healed quickly
after mending.


Simple Operation Later.


She must twist one of her legs a
little when she walks and runs, but
doctors advise against correcting
this until several years have passed.
AS she grows the leg should
straighten itself to some extent, they
say, and when Nancy Jean is about
IL, more simple operation can be
performed to complete the healing


But nothing worries Nancy Jean.
She laughs and plays throughout
the day. She never complains. She
is happy.


And Christmas Day was a doubly
happy one for her-and the older
Kurries.


Yesterday morning, the same as
almost every morning since Nancy
Jean came home from the hospital,
Mrs. Kurrie said to her husband:


ut seems almost like fairy

LIE HAVRE, France, Dec. 90
French police, cooperating with
United States consular officials,
pushed an investigation today into
a ring for smuggling aliens into the
United States. Two arrests have
been made already.


The ring was disclosed when nine
would-be stowaways emerged from
hiding places aboard the French
liner Normandie here December 8,
when the vessel was laid up by a
strike among crew members.


Police at that time discovered the
stowaways had been supplied with
food by members of the crew, work.
ing with an alien smuggling ring.


Alphonse Lizard and Robert Dago.
both of the Normandie crew, were
arrested yesterday while police
promised further arrests.

reports OF casualties followed the latest

Lusby consistently were outstanding

The baby'S father, 82-year-old

HAS YOUNG WIFE


Being father is nothing new
for George Boarman. He's been
through the experience 26 times.
But it was the first child for his
third wife, 21-year-old Mrs. Edith
William Boarman, who also was
reported doing nicely" at the hos
pital but who occupied spot in
the background in the unusual sit
uation.


Makes me feel like a kid
again. Bet folks think I'm a
crackerjack." Boarman told
newspapermen.


LOSES COUNT


Boarman's first wife bore him
Is children before she died. His
second marriage was childless.
Boarman didn't rightly know
just how many Of his children
were alive, but calculated there
were eight or ten. He said he just
couldn't tell how many grandchil-
dren he had, but added his grand
daughter, Jeanette, soon was to
present him with a great-grand-
child.


"Thatll be someone to keep
my son company and play with"
the wonder watchman observed.


The twenty-sixth Boarman
child was born Sunday.

uN.S0-In a firm, clear voice,

O'Connor, coed athlete, known to
friends as "Petey," today pleaded
"I arm not guilty" when called to
trial for the mud-puddle Staying
of five.year-old Nancy Glenn, last
Labor Day.


The 19-year-old defendant, &C.
companied by her parents, arrived
seven minutes late and had to
force her way into the jammed
courtroom of Judge Joseph Sloane.
A crowd of would-be spectators,
mostly women, attempted to fol
low the trio, but was showed back
by a special Gordon of police.


JURORS QUICKLY CHOSEN


The first juror-John Digildo,
pharmacist-was selected half
an hour after Miss O'Connor
pleaded not guilty to indictments
charging murder and voluntary
and involuntary manslaughter.


Digildo automatically became
foreman of the jury Four other
jurors were chosen in quick sue
cession. They were Joseph Bo-
rejko, butcher; Anthony Gentle,

candy coater, and Harry Wynne,
garage owner.


The girl stepped from a psyche
phatic ward to face her friend and
confidante, Mrs. Marie Kibler
Phillips, 1885 Olympic gymnast,
whose testimony may send her to
the electric chair.


CONFESSION" WITHHELD


Six years Mary's senior and a
bride of two days when the kill
ing occurred, Mrs. Phillips with
held information Of Mary's con.
fession "out of loyalty" she ex-
Jplained.


Mrs. Phillips is listed as State
witness. Both she and her hus-
band, Chester, also an Olympic
star, believe the child's death was
an accident, distorted into a
crime by Mary's emotionally up
set mind.


According to both Mrs. Phillips
and Mary's unsigned statement
to police, Little Nancy annoyed"
Mary on Labor Day and the girl
struck the child. When the child
dropped unconscious and Mary
discovered she was dead, the col.
Ilege athlete pushed the child's
face into a mudhole, attempting

nlled with spectators. The band of

The income of American corpo-
rations during the first half, even the
first three quarters of 1887, made
very happy reading. Except where
prolonged strikes had cut heavily into
production, steady and substantial
gains were being recorded over 1896
earnings. which had not been negli-
gtbie.


When production plummeted in the
fall, however, estimates OF total earn
ings for the year had to be quickly
revised Higher costs for labor and
material could not be hastily ad-
justed and operating costs for the
final quarter. will undoubtedly be
found to have cut drastioally into ex-
pected profits. Corporate income for
the whole year, nonetheless, should
show gain over 1886 and possibly
an important one.


All industries did not share alike,
naturally. The extended strikes, the
high labor costs, and the higher costs
of raw materials and parts, reduced
the earnings of automobile manufac-
turers below 1886 totals even though
more cars and trucks were sold.


Steel Has Good Year.


On the other hand, the steel in
dustry compiled remarkable ton
mage and earnings record during the
first nine months of 1887 and the
gains of this period are too great to
be Cancelled by the subsequent abrupt
fall drop in operating rate from 80
to 80 per cent. Although labor costs
were higher in steel, too, price in
creases were well absorbed during the
early part of the year and the sus-
tanned activity at high levels tended
to permit economical production.


Profits of the food manufacturers
and distributors were hit more by
rising material costs than anything
else. Mounting wholesale and COM
modify prices were not quickly re-
f1ected in retail price increases and
profit margins were cut substantially.
In contrast to other groups, food COM
panies will probably show as good or
better earnings for the last half of the
year as for the first half when the
price problem was most serious.


Fewer Extra Dividends.


The flood of special year-end divi-
dends, extras, and stock bonuses which
gladdened the hearts of investors in
the pre- Christmas season Of 1886 was
not repeated in 1887.


Some melons" mostly of minor
nature were cut but there was not
the distribution in anticipation Of
fat fourth-quarter earnings which was
the rule the year previous.


Many companies on other meet
ing dates had disbursed dividends
closely paralleling earnings and,
despite the surplus tax, it was the
general tendencies to keep reserves
as high as possible in the face OF
prevailing doubts of the future.

National Guard troops and survivor
volunteers-thoughtless of their own

Red Cross officials expressed belief

The battering power of 3O-foot tidal

lated tenement district.


Little Rhode Island remained the
focal point of relief efforts, and extra
ordinary measures were taken to pre-
vent pillaging of stores and looting OF
the dead. Flooded Providence. Woon-
socket and Westerly, where more than
100 died, were under martial law.


The w. P. A. dispatched 5000 work.
ers for rescue duty in answer to an

To keep away spectators. police roped

Cape Cod Patrolled.


Extra police patrolled Cape Cod and
the 125-mile length of Long Islands
South Shore, playground for New
York society. where footing was re-
ported. Exclusive Long Island beach
colonies, like sections of Rhode
Islands ocean front. lay in shambles


Transportation of food and cloth
ing to helpless refugees remained a
gigantic problem. Highways through
out New England were still impossible
over long distances, shipping was
crippled and communication difficult.


Several villages in Massachusetts,
Vermont and New Hampshire were
virtually isolated Power shortages
curtailed factory production. and the
abating f1oodwaters disclosed further
havoc to industrial plants.


Interruption of railroad schedules
and inability to use blocked roads for
motor transport left New York and
Boston trade terminals glutted with
supplies badly needed by New Eng
land merchants and flood sufferers


Trains moved Sporadically and many
travellers resorted to the air. In IS
trips yesterday airlines shuttled 1876
passengers between Boston and New

a new study OF the railroad industry

Surveys.

mand. should bolster grain and cotton
shipments, while the improved business
outlook heralds better industrial
traf1ic." states the survey. Intense

dering most difficult the currently

best meet the competitive problem
This would involve extensive CONSOLE
dation of railroad plant, together with

lessly improbable routes. Naturally

ing down capitalizatio but since fixed
charges now take less than 20 per cent

costs alone consume over so per cent
the greater savings must be at the ex-
pense of labor. The tremendous in
f1uence Of organized labor. however,
precludes any such accomplishments
over the near term. In fact, no wage
reductions are likely this year.


Thus. with further freight rate in
creases unlikely. the principal hope for
the railroads is rise in the volume

pect. with agricultural production
again normal and modest recovery in

to light evidence of startling crop
damage done a month or two ago by
frost and cold weather Ravages of
rust also have been barred. Excessive
rainfall has slowed the harvest and
lodged wheat

partly confirmed by experts swarming
into the belt to make new appraisals
of the crop which promised to be
the largest in the Nations history,
indicated decidedly less optimistic
prospects for bumper winter wheat
yield.


This development. coupled with the
fact that domestic prices haye risen
about IL cents bushel from the five

bullish factor. Frightened by the crop
reports and by the higher prices,

purchased in weeks. Export sales

winter wheat, and a little Canadian
grain.

port for June, released after the

surprising item. The Governments

By the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, May 1.-THE Oil in
dustry entered the second quarter this
year with earning power less affected
by the current recession than general
industry.


A recent tabulation by the National
City Bank stated the first IA report
ing petroleum producing and refining
organizations earned 81 per cent less
in the quarter ended March 81 than
a year ago. while 280 representative
companies had profits cut 81 per cent.


This industry, one Of the largest
from the standpoint of both invest
ment and value Of product, has been
favored by relatively stable crude oil
prices. Mid-Continent crude, for in
stance, was quoted yesterday at $1.16
a barrel, unchanged from last year.
For almost two years now the oil
producers have been able to sell all
their output at this fixed, compare
lively high price.


Demand Increases.


Steadily rising demand for pc
troleum products-crude oil for home
heating and gasoline for automobiles
has combined with the relatively
favorable crude price structure to
maintain earnings at high level.


The record stocks of gas
oline on hand, however, have caused
sporadic price cutting-especially in
the Middle West-and tended to de-
press profits Of concerns operating in
that section.


California companies were enabled
to chalk up the best net income in
nine years during the first three
months because gasoline prices con-
tinued firm.


A factor Of jor Importance in
bolstering the industry's profit-and-
loss performance recently was the So
called Iowa" plan of service station
management. This involved turning
over company-owned stations to inde-
pendant operators on contract basis,
enabling the producers to maintain
sales volume and at the same time
eliminating many of the problems
inherent to station operations.


Hurt by Price Wars.


One recurring malady company
owned stations were faced with was
retail price wars. Losses were wholly
borne by the parent company and
prices often slashed to disastrously
low levels. Under the Iowa plan of
operation, however, both the leasee
and the company shared the losses.


During the current recession, price
wars have remained strictly local in
character. No large company-owned
chains were involved with the wide
price shading, resulting from cuts in
one area, to bring the entire chain
in line.

frontier killing of two Germans by

horse, since such guarantees then
could not come into the negotiations

reconcile their differences.


German-speaking peoples of Czecho-

BRUSSELS. Aug. 16.-Forty thou
sand Belgian soldiers were massed
along the German frontier today for
maneuvers intended to prove this
country will never become another
Austria.


The Belgian war games, along both
the Netherlands and German borders,
were to begin today and continue
through August %.


The maneuvers will be the most
spectacular ever held in this country
and will be geared to the defense
problems of the eastern frontier, where
"a years ago this month the German
juggernaut crushed hastily modified
Belgian defenders.


Belgium's peace-time soldiers. close
knit in a highly mobile army, during
the week of war games will defend
the same route over which the Kaiser's
armies marched in 1914-a narrow
strip between Holland and Luxem-
bourg.


This little kingdom believes it has
learned lot since the World War,
and the war games are a further ef-
fort to keep defense tactics up to
date in perilous times.

GASPE TOWN, July 23.-Canada' s
Gaspe is full of delightful surprises
for the tourist, but the biggest sur
prise Of all is that this land-now so
easily reached-could preserve so we'll
its pristine beauty and antique charm.


Picturesque fishing hamlets stand
virtually unchanged from their quiet
way Of life so years ago. when there
was neither road nor rail to connect
them with the outside world. And
the great thousand-foot cliffs. the
tumbling streams. the sunny meadows,
the dense forests. and the serene
stretches of blue sky and bluer sea
have altered not whit since the days
when Cartier discovered this tower
ing headland in 1884.


Just what do you see when you tour
the Gaspe? Eastward from Ste Flavie
its the ripping St. Lawrence. dotted
with little towns growing into quiet
summer resorts like Metis Beach and
Cap Chat. Tiny houses brightly
painted every color of the rainbow to
match the brilliance OF the meadow
flowers. cluster in valley villages or
perch precariously on the edge of some
lonely crag. Farther along the road
one occasionally sees great black
cross marking a saltwater tragedy
the wreck of some ill-fated fishing
craft


Out on the river and on the blue
sWells of the Gulf of ST. Lawrence the
brown sails Of fishing boats fill with a
breeze that sets the pine trees of the
landward forests swaying and signing
At dusk the fantastic rock formations
cast strange shadows across the quiet
ing water while bell buoy tolls an
evening carlton.


On the end of the peninsula at
Gaspe Town is the Jacques Cartier
Memorial A few miles farther, Perce
affords the scenic high-spot of the
trip with its curiously eroded cliffs
like the Three Sisters, and Bonaven-
ture Island. inhabited by gulls, gan
nets and other sea birds in untold
thousands.

Associated Press Foreien Correspondent.


JAFFA. Palestine, Aug. 27.-Racial
strife between Jews and Arabs broke
into new fury today soon after cur
few was lifted.


Arab crowds. still smarting under
the disastrous market place bombing
yesterday in which "a Arabs died, at
tackled Jewish shops on the main
streets Of Jaffa and attempted to set
them afire


Their antipathy against the British
mounted when news spread that IL
Arabs had been killed and scores
wounded in a battle near Tul Karin
Two British flyers were killed when
a Royal Air Force plane crashed while
supporting British troops.


80 Arabs Killed.


Total casualties In the Holy Land
terrorism for yesterday included 38
Arabs killed and 36 wounded, Jew
ish watchman killed and seven Jews
wounded, two Britons killed and one
wounded.


Swift arrival of British forces today
frustrated further serious disturbances
in the long strife.


One Arab was killed and seven
others wounded, however, before sui
len crowds were dispersed.


Troops were rushed to all danger
spots and armored cars took positions
in Jaffa's main street, while machine
gun posts were set up to guard the
border between Jaffa and the all-Jew-
ish city of Tel Aviv. All business in
Jaffa was suspended.


Police Are Modified.


The police force modified It's full
strength to prevent further outbreaks
at Ramle, midway between Jerusalem
and Tel Aviv, after an ambulance
driver was seriously wounded.


Arabs called a strike throughout the
Holy Land in sympathy for the victims
and in protest to the government OF
the British inundated territory. Arab
shops were closed in Jerusalem and
Haifa, both Arab strongholds.


In London, the British Palestine
Commission continued its hearings on
the program for splitting the Holy
Land into an Arab state. Jewish state
and . inundated area.


The colonial Office issued state
ment on yesterdays disorders, saying
that police and military action quick
ly restored calm

E. Russell Kelly, who was appointed
yesterday by Justice Daniel w. O'Don-
oghue Of District Court to defend
Robert F. Langdon, indicted for the
Staying seven years ago Of Beulah
Limerick, today was studying the
lengthy record of the case preparatory
to deciding what tack and defense will
take.


Mr.. Kelly's appointment was dis
closed yesterday afternoon. Langdon.
when arraigned more than a week
ago, had told the court he had no
attorney and wanted the court 10
appoint one.


The Limerick murder has long been
one of Washington's most battling
mysteries. The young theater usher
ette was found dead in her own bed,
but so cleverly had the bullet wound
in her head been concealed that it
was not discovered until some time
later that she had been slain.


Langdon was held for the grand
jury shortly after the crime, but was
not indicted until about two weeks
ago, the jurors having concluded at
the time that there was insufficient
evidence to hold him


Mr.. Kelly is former assistant
United States attorney and Is well
known at the bar.

Officials recalled that the depart

April 80, 1898. But after all these
years there is still one thing puzzling
the authorities-just where the tenn
porary quarters in which the new
department was housed during its first
three years of life?


In 1901. the department said yes
terday, the organization was moved
into the old War Office, located near
the White House, on a site now occu-
pied by the southern end of the State
Department Building.


Although the War Office was de-
stroyed when the British, in 1914.
burned the National Capital, most of
the naval archives and other valuable
papers were transported to safe spot
in Georgetown.


The War Office was reconstructed
in 1916 and utilized to house the State.
War and Navy Departments. When
the former departments shifted into
new quarters four years later, the
Navy became the sole tenant of the
building.


In 1879 the Navy moved into the
east wing of the new State, War and
Navy Building, and there the greater
part of the department was housed
until the World War. With the tre-
mendous expansion then experienced,
the Navy Department in 1918 moved
into its present home on Constitution
avenue between Seventeenth and
Nineteenth streets NV.


Plans of the National Capital Park
and Planning Commission provide that
between the new Navy Department
and the Potomac River, abutting the
Rock Greek and Potomac parkway,
there will be naval museum to house
many 70 the relics that is the services
heritage through the years.

BY the Associated Press.


MADRID, July 20. - The United
States Embassy Building here was hit
by four shells early today when in
surgent artillery bombarded the city.
Some damage was caused but no one
in the Embassy Building was hurt.


Elsewhere in the city seven persons
were wounded.


The embassy has not been occupied
by diplomatic officers since early in
the war. (The Ambassador. Claude G..
de Luz, France.)


The shelling began about am.
Some of the shells, unusually large,
tore great holes in buildings and
streets. Citizens rushed from their
beds TO cellars and other shelters.


This was the first time the Embassy
had sustained a direct hit during the
nearly two years siege of Madrid.
Shell fragments and bullets frequently
had landed in the garden.


One shell crashed through the roof
of the porter'S lodge, hit the ground,
tore through a gate and exploded in
the street. Another struck a tennis
pavilion, smashed two windows and
riddled the walls with fragments.


1nsurgent Drive Slowed.


HENDAYE, France cat the Spanish
frontieD, July 20 LP).-The govern
ment,s U-shaped line of hasty de-
lenses across the Valencia
highway slowed the first wave of the
Spanish insurgents six-day offensive
today.


Dispatches from Generalissimo
Frances headquarters admitted gov
ernment resistance suddenly had stiff
fened as the militiamen's retreat
brought, them to the new defense line
Insurgents were forced hastily to
reorganize their lines. Orders were
given for an extraordinary effort on
the part of the two f1anks, on either
side OF the highway, to catch up with
the center.


The new government line to defend
Valencia against the insurgent drive
runs south from Pima. curving slowly
across the highway to the crest of
Ragudo Hill, then turns northwest
through Ell Toro Mountains.


Insurgents reported they held the
village of Ragudo itself, nesting at
the foot Of the hill five miles from
Viver, the first of three cities Franco
must take before he reaches Valencia.

hours.

Associated Press Foreign Correspondent.


WITH THE JAPANESE ARMY IN
CENTRAL CHINA, May 23.-The
Japanece field command said today
that 10000 demoralized Chinese SOL
diers have surrendered since the fall
of Suchow.


The number of prisoners mounted
rapidly as Japanese forces relentlessly
pursued fragments Of the routed Chi
nece Army fleeing from the conquered
Central China railroad zone.


FLYING over the Suchow area in a
Japanese war plane, I saw a ghastly
srSctacle of desperate, shattered Chi
nese fighting for their lives in the
Suchow trap


The japanese said they had mar
rowed the trap down to an area
= roughly IL miles in diameter. CENTER
ing on the Lushan Hills. midway be-
tween Suchow and Suhsien.


Passing over Suchow at 500 feet, 1t
could be plainly seen that the Jap
anese were in full possession of that
city, junction of the Lunghai and
Tientsin-Pukow Railways. The Ris-
ing Sun flag floated over the city and 1t
swarmed with japanese troops, tanks
and trucks.

the japanese say more than 2OO,000
Chinese were caught, tanks motorized
units and infantry could be seen pur-
suing groups of fugitives across the
fields, harrassing them with machine
gun and rifle fire.

villages, wrecked bridges, devastated

trenches.

turned into widespread open warfare,

spokesman said gap approx
mately 80 miles long still existed along

which several Chinese divisions al
ready have fled westward The jap
anese previously had claimed the Su-
chow area was completely encircled
and that the Chinese trapped there
were faced with either surrender or
humiliation.


The admission that gap remained
unclosed was taken to mean that the
Chinese still have a possible outlet to
the west and that others probably will
, escape.

of the japanese pressing their cam
paign westward along the Lunghai into

chow area were mopping up.


Purpose of this drive was to sever
the Peiping- -Hankow Railway some
where between Chengchow and Han
kow, present seat of Generalissimo
Chang Kai-shek's Central Chinese
government.

the Lunghai was aimed at Chengchow,
junction on the Lunghai and Peiping-

ernment defenses in Eastern Spain
today and advanced miles nearer
the lifeline" highway link between
Madrid and the Mediterranean ports
Of Castellon de la Plana and Valencia.

government line was broken 40 miles
north and slightly to the west of

town of Portell. deep in the pocket

coast lines.

taken by troops of Insurgent Gen.

southwest from Cinctorres, a village

tellon were the object of both opera
tions

coast and close two gateWays for sup
plies into the larger of the two seq
ments of government territory broke
the curving front of the defenders
from Teruel eastward to the sea.

government losses as coastal column
driving south toward Castellon routed
Gen. Jose Miaja's ''milicianos" from
mountain positions at bayonet point.


The defenders tried to slip through

Frances machine gunners drove them
